I. Any $4\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

II. Any matrix of the form  $A=[\begin{aligned}-a & 0 \\ 0 & a\end{aligned}]$ has exactly one negative and one positive singular value.

III. Any $2\times 4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false.  All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, 
$A$  can't have any negative singular value.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed,  since $A$ is a $2\times 4$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $4\times 4$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{4\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 4}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{4\times 4}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b4af41fc-239f-5a7e-a80b-a2420f5b8338"] :db/ensure "e5110c54-de9e-5958-ac4d-933027f79b9c" :question/math-academy-id "q-3977" :question/problem "If ${z}^{3}-5{z}^{2}=-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z$, then $z=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(z)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =-2{z}^{3}+4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-5{z}^{2} & =4{z}^{2}+30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2} & =30z \\ 3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3z.$ We can factor out the $3z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{3}-9{z}^{2}-30z & =0 \\ 3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${z}^{2}-3z-10$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z({z}^{2}-3z-10) & =0 \\ 3z(z-5)(z+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $z=0,$ $z=5,$ and $z=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields $$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{3}+45{y}^{2}+75y & =0 \\ 3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3y(2{y}^{2}+15y+25) & =0 \\ 3y(2y+5)(y+5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

"Find the roots of the polynomial $p(y)=6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(y)=0,$ that is

$$
6{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-45{y}^{2}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{y}^{2}.$ We can factor out the $3{y}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{y}^{2}+y-15$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}(2{y}^{2}+y-15) & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}(y+3)(2y-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $y=-3,$ and $y=\frac{5}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields #uuid "773cbe61-ec11-5375-8f39-d897f1cb3120" :question/math-academy-id "q-64333" :question/problem "Find ${\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$

${\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t=i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k$ 
and 
$c=i+k.$" :question/worked-solution "The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3fb741de-a765-5845-9e59-3f7b8e4242c7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073445 :question/problem "Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=4 \\ x+2y=16\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\
	y &=4
}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073753 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-498d2b3f-6756-59df-bd3d-256bb722b0aa" "question-d389f84f-6df2-5d57-9702-acb625d9c80f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073446 :question/problem "Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2u+9v-6=0 \\ 2u+6v-8=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:
![](images/77/77459b19bb1fd1f28e05e6f613e4e49af34595eae33eeeca584d65a289f7ea2c.svg)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \
2u+6v &= 8 \
2u &= 8 - 6v \
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \
u &= 4 - 3v
}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \
2+3v &= 0 \
3v &= -2 \
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \
	2u-12 &= 0 \
	2u &= 12 \
	u &= 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-07b5302b-d797-5328-827e-aa28a460f929" :question/id #uuid "07b5302b-d797-5328-827e-aa28a460f929" :question/math-academy-id "q-181149" :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations:

So, we replace $u$ with $-v-2$ in the first equation and solve for $v:$

$$

If we now substitute $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ into $u=-v-2,$ then we can find the value of $u:$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,v=-\frac{1}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e16e42d5-5e57-5702-bb36-98fb0bad0dd6" "answer-field-da300820-d65a-54b5-a122-648e1be4ca42"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e16e42d5-5e57-5702-bb36-98fb0bad0dd6" :answer-field/id #uuid "e16e42d5-5e57-5702-bb36-98fb0bad0dd6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-0db68d80-560b-5294-a3e9-812966c11801" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0db68d80-560b-5294-a3e9-812966c11801"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0db68d80-560b-5294-a3e9-812966c11801" :answer/id #uuid "0db68d80-560b-5294-a3e9-812966c11801" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-da300820-d65a-54b5-a122-648e1be4ca42" :answer-field/id #uuid "da300820-d65a-54b5-a122-648e1be4ca42" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-51c5dada-d996-51cf-94d1-ca897ceda4c8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-51c5dada-d996-51cf-94d1-ca897ceda4c8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-51c5dada-d996-51cf-94d1-ca897ceda4c8" :answer/id #uuid "51c5dada-d996-51cf-94d1-ca897ceda4c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4c3907fe-c83e-5bd5-ac54-297aa503451b" :question/id #uuid "4c3907fe-c83e-5bd5-ac54-297aa503451b" :question/math-academy-id "q-181175" :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations:

\{\begin{aligned}-2x+y=-4 \\ x-3y=-8\end{aligned}

Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $3y$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
x=3y-8
$$

So, we replace $x$ with $3y-8$ in the first equation and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =-4 \\ -2(3y-8)+y & =-4 \\ -6y+16+y & =-4 \\ -5y & =-20 \\ y & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=3y-8,$ then we can find the value of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-8 \\ x & =3(4)-8 \\ x & =12-8 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 \\ 5y-15x+10=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ca46e4e1-5150-5d40-98c3-33efe3175aed"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ca46e4e1-5150-5d40-98c3-33efe3175aed" :answer-field/id #uuid "ca46e4e1-5150-5d40-98c3-33efe3175aed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6ed3f880-96ed-5fd6-824f-be81fbff3e25" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e81c2d81-0ae0-51a8-90a5-645bcd295610" "answer-adefce60-eb41-5a32-906f-e3cd671a3daa" "answer-b6612f39-f352-56c1-817b-399df43c996f" "answer-92cf3e39-98db-564f-a3c5-ad104dff9377" "answer-6ed3f880-96ed-5fd6-824f-be81fbff3e25"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e81c2d81-0ae0-51a8-90a5-645bcd295610" :answer/id #uuid "e81c2d81-0ae0-51a8-90a5-645bcd295610" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-adefce60-eb41-5a32-906f-e3cd671a3daa" :answer/id #uuid "adefce60-eb41-5a32-906f-e3cd671a3daa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b6612f39-f352-56c1-817b-399df43c996f" :answer/id #uuid "b6612f39-f352-56c1-817b-399df43c996f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92cf3e39-98db-564f-a3c5-ad104dff9377" :answer/id #uuid "92cf3e39-98db-564f-a3c5-ad104dff9377" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6ed3f880-96ed-5fd6-824f-be81fbff3e25" :answer/id #uuid "6ed3f880-96ed-5fd6-824f-be81fbff3e25" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d389f84f-6df2-5d57-9702-acb625d9c80f" :question/id #uuid "d389f84f-6df2-5d57-9702-acb625d9c80f" :question/math-academy-id "q-181207" :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p-6q=-18 \\ 4p+3q+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution $(p,q)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

$(p,q)=($
{{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}
$)$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p-6q=-18 & \,\,(1) \\ 4p+3q+2=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(1),$ we can solve for $p$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6q & =-18 \\ 3p & =6q-18 \\ p & =2q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $p=2q-6$ into equation $(2)$ and solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(2q-6)+3q+2 & =0 \\ 8q-24+3q+2 & =0 \\ 11q & =22 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $q=2$ into equation $(1),$ then we can find the value of $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p-6(2) & =-18 \\ 3p-12 & =-18 \\ 3p & =-6 \\ p & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=-2,\,q=2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d502feb6-12a4-5b5d-a239-789af82850e4" "answer-field-ef8a675b-4a10-5910-adfc-f84ccbe5facf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d502feb6-12a4-5b5d-a239-789af82850e4" :answer-field/id #uuid "d502feb6-12a4-5b5d-a239-789af82850e4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ff409c69-65be-5db8-9082-449cc256ae35" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff409c69-65be-5db8-9082-449cc256ae35"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff409c69-65be-5db8-9082-449cc256ae35" :answer/id #uuid "ff409c69-65be-5db8-9082-449cc256ae35" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ef8a675b-4a10-5910-adfc-f84ccbe5facf" :answer-field/id #uuid "ef8a675b-4a10-5910-adfc-f84ccbe5facf" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-be1f5640-6243-5fce-a7c7-5b82c5d69ef4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-be1f5640-6243-5fce-a7c7-5b82c5d69ef4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-be1f5640-6243-5fce-a7c7-5b82c5d69ef4" :answer/id #uuid "be1f5640-6243-5fce-a7c7-5b82c5d69ef4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y=4 \\ x-2=y\,\end{aligned}
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073923 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124591 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/id #uuid "b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/math-academy-id "q-94614" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2,$ and its subset $A$ containing all polynomials of the form $a{t}^{2},$ where $a\in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{2}$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{2}$ are two polynomials from $A,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & ={a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{a}_{2}{t}^{2} \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(t)=a{t}^{2}\in A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =k(a{t}^{2}) \\  & =(ka){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf373aed-aad4-52b7-aa07-ba88e991e0e8"] :db/ensure "426d96cd-8cff-562b-8539-4a443da3b8d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-80668" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A$, where

$$

and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(0,1)\times (0,1)$ and ${R}_{2}=(0,1)\times (1,2).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}2x\text{ }\,{e}^{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-0){\int }_{0}^{1}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & ={x}^{3}{|}_{0}^{1}+({x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1})\cdot ({e}^{y}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =1+1\cdot ({e}^{2}-{e}^{1}) \\  & =1+{e}^{2}-e.\end{aligned}

"question-07d5c9c5-374d-5c01-b3ec-d01486174f96" :question/id #uuid "07d5c9c5-374d-5c01-b3ec-d01486174f96" :question/math-academy-id "q-161744" :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](images/d2/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-851dbeb9-5199-5c05-92dd-f09fe944b1b4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "b06611cf-54db-58f0-8277-482f7aa27724" :question/math-academy-id "q-161753" :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{5}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bb52fe98-2353-5c03-b8bc-f23854e8e611"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}:$

$$

$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{4}\,d\rho  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{\rho }^{5}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2}\,d\rho  \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{32}{5} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{15}\end{aligned}

:question/problem "![](images/2f/2fd023af7c229d813344ee366b384a5917b69df0d06fabff6466b9ebcc199bb9.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ for $y\le 0$ and $z\le 0,$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](images/09/090f210768ffd4a6be529860b54a2906e265427b7d85bcbb07e3101c801740ba.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{4}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{\rho }^{6}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=\pi /2}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =\pi }^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{7}{\rho }^{7}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2} \\  & =-(-1-0)\cdot (2\pi -\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{7}(128-0) \\  & =1\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{128}{7} \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0f2e7f56-ee2d-5dfd-af32-c2c72dce6d2b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "![](images/4d/4d2a71ffdce7f02cdfa78881c7e355c9aada4134cf06b663a2deefb3d779b9ca.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =8x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =8\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/04/0475e2e272a30318dc4cb31457539a312544b6e14d7e6a8ed3f911d41404b575.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2cbd266d-a5fa-5b3b-84b2-668b33154b73"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x-3xy=0 \\ -5y+4xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3xy & =0 \\ x(2-3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4xy & =0 \\ y(-5+4x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(-5+4x) & =0 \\ -5+4x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164545 :answer-field/correct "answer-9f5c3169-d779-521a-8197-1104e5c087d6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9f5c3169-d779-521a-8197-1104e5c087d6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f5c3169-d779-521a-8197-1104e5c087d6" :answer/id #uuid "9f5c3169-d779-521a-8197-1104e5c087d6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164546 :answer-field/correct "answer-a18a65b5-78bf-5bcc-a5ae-bc42d6062064" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a18a65b5-78bf-5bcc-a5ae-bc42d6062064"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a18a65b5-78bf-5bcc-a5ae-bc42d6062064" :answer/id #uuid "a18a65b5-78bf-5bcc-a5ae-bc42d6062064" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370181 :question/problem "$$

$\{\begin{aligned}x=-t \\ y=t, \\ z=t\end{aligned}$ where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$" :question/worked-solution "Substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}+3{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2} & =2 \\ (-t)^{2}+2(t)^{2}+6(t)^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}+6{t}^{2} & =2 \\ 9{t}^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$ and $t=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ y=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ z=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).$

- For $t=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).$

:question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
\frac{x-8}{4}=y=z=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=4t+8 \\ y=t \\ z=t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =3{z}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2}+3{t}^{2} & =3{t}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+8 & =0 \\ 4t & =-8 \\ t & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line. For $t=-2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(-2)+8=0 \\ y=-2 \\ z=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,-2,-2).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/id #uuid "ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-94789" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the elliptic cone $3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2{z}^{2}$ and the line $\frac{x+12}{3}=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
\frac{x+12}{3}=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{4}=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=3t-12 \\ y=4t \\ z=4t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =2{z}^{2} \\ 3(3t-12)^{2}+2(4t)^{2} & =2(4t)^{2} \\ 3(3t-12)^{2} & =0 \\ (3t-12)^{2} & =0 \\ 3t-12 & =0 \\ 3t & =12 \\ t & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solution back into the equations of the line. For $t=4,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=3(4)-12=0 \\ y=4(4)=16 \\ z=4(4)=16.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/id #uuid "8c16a549-c615-5f5a-9201-b01b9bbc4908" :question/math-academy-id "q-36325" :question/problem "Find the projection of the intersection between the hyperboloid of one sheet

 and the plane   $x+2z=-3$ onto the
$xy$-plane." :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $z$, as follows:

$$
x+2z=-3\,⟹\,z=-\frac{x+3}{2}
$$

Substituting the expression for $z$ into the equation of the hyperboloid, we obtain: 

$$

\{\begin{aligned}3u+z=-2 \\ (\,3u-5z=-17\,)\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3u+z=-2 \\ -3u+5z=17\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3u}+z & =-2 \\ -\cancel{3u}+5z & =17 \\ (z+5z) & =(-2+17) \\ 6z & =15 \\ z & =\frac{15}{6} \\ z & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}

So, the solution must have $z=\frac{5}{2}.$ However, we still need to find $u.$ To do this, we substitute $z=\frac{5}{2}$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3u+z & =-2 \\ 3u+\frac{5}{2} & =-2 \\ 3u & =-\frac{9}{2} \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,z=\frac{5}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :answer/id #uuid "157119ad-5b76-548f-a94f-bee7025201f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(3,-5)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084514 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without using graphs*, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y=1 \\ 5x-y=11\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we must combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation. One way to combine the equations is to use the **elimination method.** 

Notice that the coefficient of $y$ in the first equation is $1,$ and the coefficient of $y$ in the second equation is $-1.$ Since these numbers add to zero, we can *add* the two equations, *eliminate* the variable $y,$ and solve the resulting equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{y} & =1 \\ 5x-\cancel{y} & =11 \\ (x+5x) & =(1+11) \\ 6x & =12 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=2.$ However, we still need to find $y.$ To do this, we substitute $x=2$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+y & =1 \\ (2)+y & =1 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=2$ and $y=-1,$ which can be expressed as $(2, -1).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186084515 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that we want to solve the following system of linear equations using elimination:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=1 \\ x-y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/85/85996afab1889f8032a295f4db6bbbcbc8670a0bc12f0b64f53a3b809f111628.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This eliminates the variable $x,$ making it possible to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083433 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198405 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/id #uuid "a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99271" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=y-3x$ given that  ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 250.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=250.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=250
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{3}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-3y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-3y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ 9{y}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ {y}^{2} & =25 \\ y & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-3y=∓15.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-15,5),\,(15,-5).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-15,5)$ | $(15,-5)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $50$ | $-50$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-15,5),$ and its maximum value is $50.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bd28c84e-3672-589b-b259-7ab643cdcbfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bd28c84e-3672-589b-b259-7ab643cdcbfc" :answer-field/id #uuid "bd28c84e-3672-589b-b259-7ab643cdcbfc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2581670b-66e9-5d37-9926-806360eb8f15" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b0a20fa1-2478-557f-919f-c382ef996ee9" "answer-4d7fc2e4-a9ae-57b1-a57d-6f3e9b58edf7" "answer-5b25f91e-47c0-5de9-8785-cc22a420cdde" "answer-280f9803-91c8-596b-9d69-7a1755e015d0" "answer-2581670b-66e9-5d37-9926-806360eb8f15"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b0a20fa1-2478-557f-919f-c382ef996ee9" :answer/id #uuid "b0a20fa1-2478-557f-919f-c382ef996ee9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d7fc2e4-a9ae-57b1-a57d-6f3e9b58edf7" :answer/id #uuid "4d7fc2e4-a9ae-57b1-a57d-6f3e9b58edf7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "15" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b25f91e-47c0-5de9-8785-cc22a420cdde" :answer/id #uuid "5b25f91e-47c0-5de9-8785-cc22a420cdde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "45" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-280f9803-91c8-596b-9d69-7a1755e015d0" :answer/id #uuid "280f9803-91c8-596b-9d69-7a1755e015d0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2581670b-66e9-5d37-9926-806360eb8f15" :answer/id #uuid "2581670b-66e9-5d37-9926-806360eb8f15" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "50" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186362354 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$

$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=35.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=35
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨8,-3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}8=4\lambda x \\ -3=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-4y\end{aligned}

Substituting $x=-4y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=35,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =35 \\ 32{y}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =35 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-4y=∓4.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-4,1),\,(4,-1).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-4,1)$ | $(4,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-35$ | $35$ |

 

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(4,-1),$ and its maximum value is $35.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281543 :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}=25.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=25
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-16y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,10y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=2\lambda x \\ -16y=10\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-\lambda )=0 \\ -2y(8+5\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,x=\pm 5,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 5,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),\,(5,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm \sqrt{5})$ | $(\pm 5,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-40$ | $25$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),$ and its minimum value is $-40.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281547 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda yz \\ 1=\lambda xz \\ 1=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281548 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ -2y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\lambda x=\frac{1}{2} \\ y(1+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,x=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-1$ in the second equation of the system, the first equation of the system gives 

$$
-x=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 2,0),\,(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{17}{4}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(2,0),$ and its maximum value is $2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-5b35fc89-ed07-5713-aff2-bd03957018fe" :activity/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=5{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2} & ∼N(5{\mu }_{1}-4{\mu }_{2},{5}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(5{\mu }_{1}-4{\mu }_{2},25{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+16{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(5\cdot 10+(-4)\cdot 20,25\cdot {3}^{2}+16\cdot {5}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-30,625).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu = -30$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{625} = 25.$ 

We want to find $P(3 \lt Y \lt  40).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =P(\frac{3-(-30)}{25}<Z<\frac{40-(-30)}{25}) \\  & =P(1.32<Z<2.8) \\  & =P(Z<2.8)-P(Z<1.32) \\  & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.32) & ≈0.9066 \\ Φ(2.8) & ≈0.9974.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32) \\  & ≈0.9974-0.9066 \\  & ≈0.09.\end{aligned}

$$
P( X+Y > 150).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X\sim N(67,12^2)$ and $Y\sim N(73,9^2),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(67+73,{12}^{2}+{9}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(140,225).\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu = 140$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{225} = 15.$

In order to find $P(X+Y > 150),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>150) & =P(Z>\frac{150-140}{15}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.67) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.67) \\  & =1-Φ(0.67)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\Phi(0.67 )\approx 0.7486.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>150) & ≈1-Φ(0.67) \\  & ≈1-0.7486 \\  & =0.2514.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the combined score is more than $150$ is $0.2514.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/id #uuid "90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-109665" :question/problem "If ${X}_{1}∼N(5,2)$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(-3,1),$ then what is the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$  then

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-20$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{625}=25.$ 

We want to find $P(-28<Y\le 12).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-28<Y\le 12) & =P(\frac{-28+20}{25}<Z\le \frac{12+20}{25}) \\  & =P(-0.32\le Z\le 1.28) \\  & =P(Z<1.28)-P(Z<-0.32) \\  & =Φ(1.28)-Φ(-0.32)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.32) & ≈0.3745 \\ Φ(1.28) & ≈0.8997.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(7-6,1+3) \\  & ∼N(1,4).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 2.1) & =P(Z\le \frac{2.1-1}{2}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.55) \\  & =Φ(0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Φ(0.55)≈0.7088.
$$

$$
P(Y\le 2.1)≈0.71.

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=2{X}_{1}-3{X}_{2} & ∼N(2{\mu }_{1}-3{\mu }_{2},4{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+9{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(4-3,28+36) \\  & ∼N(1,64).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =1$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{64}=8.$ 

We want to find $P(-4.6<Y<3.48).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.6<Y<3.48) & =P(\frac{-4.6-1}{8}<Z<\frac{3.48-1}{8}) \\  & =P(-0.70<Z<0.31) \\  & =P(Z<0.31)-P(Z<-0.70) \\  & =Φ(0.31)-Φ(-0.70)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.31) & ≈0.6217 \\ Φ(-0.70) & ≈0.2420.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.6<Y<3.48) & ≈Φ(0.31)-Φ(-0.70) \\  & ≈0.6217-0.2420 \\  & ≈0.3797.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158942 :answer-field/correct 17592186158943 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/id #uuid "f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/math-academy-id "q-109671" :question/problem "If ${X}_{1}∼N(8,{40}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(30,{30}^{2})$ are independent and $Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2},$ calculate $P(-31\le Y\le 31).$ Round your final answer to two decimal places.

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(8-30,{40}^{2}+{30}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-22,2500).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-22$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{2500}=50.$ 

We want to find $P(-31\le Y\le 31).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-31\le Y\le 31) & =P(\frac{-31-(-22)}{50}\le Z\le \frac{31-(-22)}{50}) \\  & =P(-0.18\le Z\le 1.06) \\  & =P(Z<1.06)-P(Z<-0.18) \\  & =Φ(1.06)-Φ(-0.18)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.18) & ≈0.4286 \\ Φ(1.06) & ≈0.8554\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-31\le Y\le 31) & =Φ(1.06)-Φ(-0.18) \\  & ≈0.8554-0.4286 \\  & ≈0.43.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6397adad-43cc-59f3-a17a-dddd5e5332c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The weight of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $80\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $31\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weight of the rubber is normally distributed with a mean of $45\,\text{g}$ grams and a variance of $50\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ If one racket is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $128\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5398\,$ | $\,0.5438\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ | $\,0.5517\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of the blade, and let $Y$ denote the weight of the rubber. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>128).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(80,31)$ and $Y∼N(45,50),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(80+45,31+50) \\  & ∼N(125,81).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =125$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{81}=9.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>128),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & =P(Z>\frac{128-125}{9}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.33) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.33) \\  & =Φ(0.33)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.33)≈0.6293.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & ≈1-Φ(0.33) \\  & ≈1-0.6293 \\  & ≈0.3707.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-23eb8fea-b998-548f-a61c-cbabe9a91a03"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-23eb8fea-b998-548f-a61c-cbabe9a91a03" :answer-field/id #uuid "23eb8fea-b998-548f-a61c-cbabe9a91a03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-09de9872-6ab1-5e3a-a36a-ad0d1711044d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-09de9872-6ab1-5e3a-a36a-ad0d1711044d" "answer-d0a109a1-7fb3-53b4-9819-0e61d9c1e053" "answer-3a56d3b4-a632-5cfa-b0ad-7cecce636e2f" "answer-785ba3d5-a85c-5689-b7d9-75e025455242" "answer-a2e85dc2-1f34-5360-b990-3d51b751b711"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-09de9872-6ab1-5e3a-a36a-ad0d1711044d" :answer/id #uuid "09de9872-6ab1-5e3a-a36a-ad0d1711044d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3707" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d0a109a1-7fb3-53b4-9819-0e61d9c1e053" :answer/id #uuid "d0a109a1-7fb3-53b4-9819-0e61d9c1e053" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3783" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3a56d3b4-a632-5cfa-b0ad-7cecce636e2f" :answer/id #uuid "3a56d3b4-a632-5cfa-b0ad-7cecce636e2f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4129" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-785ba3d5-a85c-5689-b7d9-75e025455242" :answer/id #uuid "785ba3d5-a85c-5689-b7d9-75e025455242" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4207" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a2e85dc2-1f34-5360-b990-3d51b751b711" :answer/id #uuid "a2e85dc2-1f34-5360-b990-3d51b751b711" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.4522" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e7f40d31-3891-595e-9dc0-80e5713161b9" :question/id #uuid "e7f40d31-3891-595e-9dc0-80e5713161b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-109757" :question/problem "A particular shop sells chickens and turkeys. The weight of a chicken is normally distributed with a mean of $1.5\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $0.1\,\text{kg}.$ The weight of a turkey is normally distributed with a mean of $8\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $0.4\,\text{kg}.$ If a chicken and a turkey are randomly selected, what is the probability that $5$ times the weight of the chicken is greater than the turkey's weight? You may assume that the weights are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ | $\,0.7852\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ | $\,0.8051\,$ | $\,0.8078\,$ | $\,0.8106\,$ | $\,0.8133\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ | $\,0.8315\,$ | $\,0.8340\,$ | $\,0.8365\,$ | $\,0.8389\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of a chicken, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a turkey. We want to find 

$$
P(5X>Y)=P(5X-Y>0).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(1.5,{0.1}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(8,{0.4}^{2}),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}5X-Y & ∼N(5\cdot 1.5-8,{5}^{2}\cdot {0.1}^{2}+{0.4}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-0.5,0.41).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $5X-Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-0.5$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.41}.$

To find $P(5X-Y>0),$ we convert $5X-Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5X-Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0-(-0.5)}{\sqrt{0.41}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.78) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.78) \\  & =1-Φ(0.78)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.78)≈0.7823.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5X-Y>0) & ≈1-Φ(0.78) \\  & ≈1-0.7823 \\  & 0.2177.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-76f631c0-460f-51ec-9363-bfa37aabf5c3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-76f631c0-460f-51ec-9363-bfa37aabf5c3" :answer-field/id #uuid "76f631c0-460f-51ec-9363-bfa37aabf5c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3beb759e-3832-5b91-8bb0-5fe04a4c0eb3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-72ce0fe1-3792-56d6-8c38-71a07f2ff7ca" "answer-cee6069b-3ea8-5bd5-9b1b-39d0ed56f8fe" "answer-0b27ab74-19c6-52de-9b88-0b5d2b3023d3" "answer-3beb759e-3832-5b91-8bb0-5fe04a4c0eb3" "answer-a683289d-1445-55db-90cf-1e6eff679e06"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-72ce0fe1-3792-56d6-8c38-71a07f2ff7ca" :answer/id #uuid "72ce0fe1-3792-56d6-8c38-71a07f2ff7ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1660" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cee6069b-3ea8-5bd5-9b1b-39d0ed56f8fe" :answer/id #uuid "cee6069b-3ea8-5bd5-9b1b-39d0ed56f8fe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1867" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b27ab74-19c6-52de-9b88-0b5d2b3023d3" :answer/id #uuid "0b27ab74-19c6-52de-9b88-0b5d2b3023d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1949" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3beb759e-3832-5b91-8bb0-5fe04a4c0eb3" :answer/id #uuid "3beb759e-3832-5b91-8bb0-5fe04a4c0eb3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2177" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a683289d-1445-55db-90cf-1e6eff679e06" :answer/id #uuid "a683289d-1445-55db-90cf-1e6eff679e06" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.2266" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-bb6e266d-fd9f-5c8c-82b7-fde74e3fe145" :question/id #uuid "bb6e266d-fd9f-5c8c-82b7-fde74e3fe145" :question/math-academy-id "q-175476" :question/problem "A particular shop sells watermelons and melons. The weight of a watermelon is normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $4\,\text{kg}.$ The weight of a melon is normally distributed with a mean of $5\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{kg}.$ If one watermelon and one melon are randomly selected, what is the probability that the weight of the watermelon is more than $3$ times greater than the weight of the melon? You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ | $\,0.7123\,$ | $\,0.7157\,$ | $\,0.7190\,$ | $\,0.7224\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ | $\,0.7454\,$ | $\,0.7486\,$ | $\,0.7517\,$ | $\,0.7549\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ | $\,0.7852\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of a watermelon, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a melon. We want to find 

$$
P(X>3Y)=P(X-3Y>0).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(10,{4}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(5,{2}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X-3Y & ∼N(10-3\cdot 5,16+{3}^{2}\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(-5,52).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X-3Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-5$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{52}.$

In order to find $P(X-3Y>0),$ we convert $X-3Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-3Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0+5}{\sqrt{52}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.69) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.69) \\  & =1-Φ(0.69)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.69)≈0.7549.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-3Y>0) & ≈1-Φ(0.69) \\  & ≈1-0.7549 \\  & ≈0.2451.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the weight of a watermelon is more than $3$ times greater than the weight of a melon is $0.2451.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard "0c9343e5-40f1-5766-8346-83637c7ee445" :question/math-academy-id "q-109759" :question/problem "In a technical support call center, waiting times are normally distributed with a mean of $15$ minutes and a standard deviation of $3$ minutes. The conversation times are normally distributed with a mean of $10$ minutes and a standard deviation of $4$ minutes. The time to solve a problem is the sum of the waiting time and the conversation time. What is the probability that it took more than $30$ minutes to solve the problem of a randomly selected caller? You may assume that waiting and conversation times are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8413\,$ | $\,0.8438\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8643\,$ | $\,0.8665\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8849\,$ | $\,0.8869\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the waiting time, and let $Y$ denote the conversation time. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>30).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(15,{3}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(10,{4}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(15+10,{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(25,25).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =25$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{25}=5.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>30),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =P(Z>\frac{30-25}{5}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1) \\  & =1-Φ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1)≈0.8413.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =1-Φ(1) \\  & ≈1-0.8413 \\  & ≈0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b619dfd9-b2dd-59c0-870d-da366a920039"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b619dfd9-b2dd-59c0-870d-da366a920039" :answer-field/id #uuid "b619dfd9-b2dd-59c0-870d-da366a920039" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-bee4b9cc-203d-5c1c-bc20-21d933ffd030" :answer-field/choices ["answer-24120408-2087-55b0-b11d-72781143b0e9" "answer-85c254a0-62c2-59a8-886c-22c3f672d045" "answer-9eff9744-fffc-5560-b024-8d235dec8231" "answer-a4b71db8-fce7-543b-b560-c183dd798dc6" "answer-bee4b9cc-203d-5c1c-bc20-21d933ffd030"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-24120408-2087-55b0-b11d-72781143b0e9" :answer/id #uuid "24120408-2087-55b0-b11d-72781143b0e9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1093" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85c254a0-62c2-59a8-886c-22c3f672d045" :answer/id #uuid "85c254a0-62c2-59a8-886c-22c3f672d045" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1112" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9eff9744-fffc-5560-b024-8d235dec8231" :answer/id #uuid "9eff9744-fffc-5560-b024-8d235dec8231" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1335" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4b71db8-fce7-543b-b560-c183dd798dc6" :answer/id #uuid "a4b71db8-fce7-543b-b560-c183dd798dc6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1357" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bee4b9cc-203d-5c1c-bc20-21d933ffd030" :answer/id #uuid "bee4b9cc-203d-5c1c-bc20-21d933ffd030" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.1587" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162297 :question/problem "A shop sells spray foam in small and large cans. The volume of liquid in a small can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.3\,\text{ltrs}$ and a standard deviation of $0.003\,\text{ltrs}.$ The volume of liquid in a large can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.6\,\text{ltrs}$ and a standard deviation of $0.008\,\text{ltrs}.$

The foam from a small can expands $40$ times its liquid volume after being sprayed in place, while the foam from a large can expands to $60$ times its liquid volume. 
If one small and one large can are randomly selected, what is the probability that the total foam volume from both cans after expanding is less than $49\,\text{ltrs}?$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |

| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the volume of liquid in a small can, and let $Y$ denote the volume of liquid in a big can. We want to find 

$$
P(40X+60Y<49).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(0.3,{0.003}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(0.6,{0.008}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}40X+60Y & ∼N(40\cdot 0.3+60\cdot 0.6,{40}^{2}\cdot {0.003}^{2}+{60}^{2}\cdot {0.008}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(48,0.2448).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $40X+60Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =48$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.2448}.$

In order to find $P(40X+60Y<49),$ we convert $40X+60Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(40X+60Y<49) & =P(Z<\frac{49-48}{\sqrt{0.2448}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<2.02) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.02) \\  & =Φ(2.02)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.02)≈0.9783.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(40X+60Y<49) & ≈Φ(2.02) \\  & ≈0.9783.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that, after expanding, the total volume of foam is less than $49$ liters is $0.9783.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158984 :answer-field/correct 17592186158986 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163271 :tutorial/content "Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be *independent* random variables that are normally distributed with

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =k(\frac{(0)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(0)^{3}}{3})+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=6\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =k(\frac{(6)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(6)^{3}}{3})+6 \\ 0 & =k(324-360)+6 \\ 0 & =-36k+6 \\ 36k & =6 \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5a78871b-3da5-52c1-a57c-cb87914fafa1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/60/602ef5480fe59ccf921d17a19d10848a1a8a04a1fc3fb3181b8e9b17ebe81fad.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(7-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(7-x) & =0 \\ 7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(7-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(7-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(7(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{10})^{2} & =k(7(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+8 \\ 20 & =12k+8 \\ 12k & =12 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =14x-{x}^{2}+16 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(7)=\sqrt{-(7)^{2}+14(7)+16}=\sqrt{65}\,m/s
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-096d2af6-6379-5a37-9ed1-9857796a70e5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/73/73da2be2514373e6d0b1052f0eca21c339b4d826d38621faf72b3e251d7d8a95.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(4-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(4-2x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(4-2x) & =0 \\ 4-2x & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=2\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2k>0$ | $0$ | $-2k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=2\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(4-2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(4-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(4(0)-(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =k(4(1)-{(1)}^{2})+8 \\ 32 & =3k+8 \\ 3k & =24 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =32x-8{x}^{2}+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =-16{x}^{2}+64x+16 \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(2)=4\sqrt{-(2)^{2}+4(2)+1}=4\sqrt{5}\,m/s
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-10849e2a-d2b8-5eda-a82b-458c2096cbcd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
