["question-773cbe61-ec11-5375-8f39-d897f1cb3120" :question/problem "Find ${\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t=i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k$ 
and 
$c=i+k.$"] ["question-773cbe61-ec11-5375-8f39-d897f1cb3120" :question/worked-solution "The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-773cbe61-ec11-5375-8f39-d897f1cb3120" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3fb741de-a765-5845-9e59-3f7b8e4242c7" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\{\begin{aligned}x-y=4 \\ x+2y=16\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186073445 :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\
	y &=4
}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$"] [17592186073446 :question/problem "Solve the following system of equations:

$$

So, we replace $x$ with $3y-8$ in the first equation and solve for $y:$

$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=3y-8,$ then we can find the value of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3y-8 \\ x & =3(4)-8 \\ x & =12-8 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

["question-498d2b3f-6756-59df-bd3d-256bb722b0aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-112214"] ["question-498d2b3f-6756-59df-bd3d-256bb722b0aa" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $y-x?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 \\ 5y-15x+10=0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-498d2b3f-6756-59df-bd3d-256bb722b0aa" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y=0 & \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10=0 & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$"] ["question-498d2b3f-6756-59df-bd3d-256bb722b0aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-ca46e4e1-5150-5d40-98c3-33efe3175aed" :answer-field/id #uuid :knowledge-point/questions "question-d389f84f-6df2-5d57-9702-acb625d9c80f"] [17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y=4 \\ x-2=y\,\end{aligned}
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable."] [17592186073923 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0] ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/id #uuid "b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91"] ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/math-academy-id "q-94614"] ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2,$ and its subset $A$ containing all polynomials of the form $a{t}^{2},$ where $a\in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $A$ is a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$

IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{2}[t]$"] ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(t)={a}_{1}{t}^{2}$ and $g(t)={a}_{2}{t}^{2}$ are two polynomials from $A,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & ={a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{a}_{2}{t}^{2} \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2}){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(t)=a{t}^{2}\in A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =k(a{t}^{2}) \\  & =(ka){t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""] ["question-b24b6cb2-194b-5c78-a36d-8250b69a2b91" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-07d5c9c5-374d-5c01-b3ec-d01486174f96" :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $x\ge 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$"] ["question-07d5c9c5-374d-5c01-b3ec-d01486174f96" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](images/d2/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-07d5c9c5-374d-5c01-b3ec-d01486174f96" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-851dbeb9-5199-5c05-92dd-f09fe944b1b4" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-c2868a77-a9f6-5df5-bf81-a733f20b3a9a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161765"] ["question-c2868a77-a9f6-5df5-bf81-a733f20b3a9a" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4.$"] ["question-c2868a77-a9f6-5df5-bf81-a733f20b3a9a" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4$ for $y\le 0$ and $z\le 0,$ shown above."] ["question-c4c2ec08-50ad-518f-bd3d-48075268a2f3" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](images/09/090f210768ffd4a6be529860b54a2906e265427b7d85bcbb07e3101c801740ba.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{2}:$

\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{4}\end{aligned}

$$"] ["question-c4c2ec08-50ad-518f-bd3d-48075268a2f3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0f2e7f56-ee2d-5dfd-af32-c2c72dce6d2b" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

["question-6022ca77-a6e7-5c06-a55c-446e2e02d3c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-71123"] ["question-6022ca77-a6e7-5c06-a55c-446e2e02d3c5" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the ellipsoid $\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}+3{z}^{2}=1$ and the line 
$\{\begin{aligned}x=-t \\ y=t, \\ z=t\end{aligned}$ where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"] ["question-6022ca77-a6e7-5c06-a55c-446e2e02d3c5" :question/worked-solution "Substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}+3{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2} & =2 \\ (-t)^{2}+2(t)^{2}+6(t)^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}+6{t}^{2} & =2 \\ 9{t}^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$ and $t=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ y=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ z=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).$

- For $t=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ z=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).$

$$
\frac{x-8}{4}=y=z=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=4t+8 \\ y=t \\ z=t,\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =3{z}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2}+3{t}^{2} & =3{t}^{2} \\ (4t+8)^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+8 & =0 \\ 4t & =-8 \\ t & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line. For $t=-2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(-2)+8=0 \\ y=-2 \\ z=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,-2,-2).$"] ["question-ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/id #uuid "ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf"] ["question-ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-94789"] ["question-ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the elliptic cone $3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2{z}^{2}$ and the line $\frac{x+12}{3}=\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{4}.$"] ["question-ac5f0783-86c6-5b1d-9dbf-c5b648b83eaf" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$

$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =2{z}^{2} \\ 3(3t-12)^{2}+2(4t)^{2} & =2(4t)^{2} \\ 3(3t-12)^{2} & =0 \\ (3t-12)^{2} & =0 \\ 3t-12 & =0 \\ 3t & =12 \\ t & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solution back into the equations of the line. For $t=4,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=3(4)-12=0 \\ y=4(4)=16 \\ z=4(4)=16.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3u+z=-2 \\ (\,3u-5z=-17\,)\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3u+z=-2 \\ -3u+5z=17\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{3u}+z & =-2 \\ -\cancel{3u}+5z & =17 \\ (z+5z) & =(-2+17) \\ 6z & =15 \\ z & =\frac{15}{6} \\ z & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $z=\frac{5}{2}.$ However, we still need to find $u.$ To do this, we substitute $z=\frac{5}{2}$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3u+z & =-2 \\ 3u+\frac{5}{2} & =-2 \\ 3u & =-\frac{9}{2} \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

"question-19d2dbdd-1890-5f16-8c5e-f4b760789d4e"] [17592186084514 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without using graphs*, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y=1 \\ 5x-y=11\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we must combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation. One way to combine the equations is to use the **elimination method.** 

Notice that the coefficient of $y$ in the first equation is $1,$ and the coefficient of $y$ in the second equation is $-1.$ Since these numbers add to zero, we can *add* the two equations, *eliminate* the variable $y,$ and solve the resulting equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{y} & =1 \\ 5x-\cancel{y} & =11 \\ (x+5x) & =(1+11) \\ 6x & =12 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=2.$ However, we still need to find $y.$ To do this, we substitute $x=2$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+y & =1 \\ (2)+y & =1 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=2$ and $y=-1,$ which can be expressed as $(2, -1).$"] [17592186084515 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that we want to solve the following system of linear equations using elimination:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=1 \\ x-y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/85/85996afab1889f8032a295f4db6bbbcbc8670a0bc12f0b64f53a3b809f111628.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This eliminates the variable $x,$ making it possible to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$"] [17592186083433 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/id #uuid "a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4"] ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99271"] ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=y-3x$ given that  ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 250.$"] ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=250.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=250
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{3}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-3y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-3y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ 9{y}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ {y}^{2} & =25 \\ y & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-3y=∓15.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-15,5),\,(15,-5).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-15,5)$ | $(15,-5)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $50$ | $-50$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-15,5),$ and its maximum value is $50.$"] ["question-a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),$ and its minimum value is $-40.$"] [17592186281547 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda yz \\ 1=\lambda xz \\ 1=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186281548 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ -2y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\lambda x=\frac{1}{2} \\ y(1+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,x=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-1$ in the second equation of the system, the first equation of the system gives 

$$
-x=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 2,0),\,(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{17}{4}$ |

$$
aX_1+bX_2\sim N(a\mu_1+b\mu_2, a^2\sigma^2_1+b^2\sigma^2_2).
$$

Since $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=5{X}_{1}-4{X}_{2} & ∼N(5{\mu }_{1}-4{\mu }_{2},{5}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}\cdot {\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(5{\mu }_{1}-4{\mu }_{2},25{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+16{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(5\cdot 10+(-4)\cdot 20,25\cdot {3}^{2}+16\cdot {5}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-30,625).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu = -30$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{625} = 25.$ 

We want to find $P(3 \lt Y \lt  40).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =P(\frac{3-(-30)}{25}<Z<\frac{40-(-30)}{25}) \\  & =P(1.32<Z<2.8) \\  & =P(Z<2.8)-P(Z<1.32) \\  & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.32) & ≈0.9066 \\ Φ(2.8) & ≈0.9974.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<Y<40) & =Φ(2.8)-Φ(1.32) \\  & ≈0.9974-0.9066 \\  & ≈0.09.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186161861 :question/problem "The math test results of a group of students are normally distributed with a mean of $67$ and a standard deviation of $12.$ The results of the same group on a history test are normally distributed with a mean of $73$ and a standard deviation of $9.$ If one student is randomly selected, what is the probability their combined score from both tests is more than $150?$ You may assume that the student's scores on both tests are independent.

$$
P( X+Y > 150).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X\sim N(67,12^2)$ and $Y\sim N(73,9^2),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(67+73,{12}^{2}+{9}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(140,225).\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu = 140$ and standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{225} = 15.$

In order to find $P(X+Y > 150),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>150) & =P(Z>\frac{150-140}{15}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.67) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.67) \\  & =1-Φ(0.67)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\Phi(0.67 )\approx 0.7486.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>150) & ≈1-Φ(0.67) \\  & ≈1-0.7486 \\  & =0.2514.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that the combined score is more than $150$ is $0.2514.$"] ["question-90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/id #uuid "90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6"] ["question-90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-109665"] ["question-90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/problem "If ${X}_{1}∼N(5,2)$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(-3,1),$ then what is the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2}?$"] ["question-90934eb8-cbb7-5339-bda4-6344e0c742e6" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$  then

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-14-6,400+225) \\  & ∼N(-20,625).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-20$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{625}=25.$ 

We want to find $P(-28<Y\le 12).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-28<Y\le 12) & =P(\frac{-28+20}{25}<Z\le \frac{12+20}{25}) \\  & =P(-0.32\le Z\le 1.28) \\  & =P(Z<1.28)-P(Z<-0.32) \\  & =Φ(1.28)-Φ(-0.32)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.32) & ≈0.3745 \\ Φ(1.28) & ≈0.8997.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-28<Y\le 12) & =Φ(1.28)-Φ(-0.32) \\  & ≈0.8997-0.3745 \\  & ≈0.53.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e193207c-9362-5624-9544-44b526952e2a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d625ba35-2bd7-5f82-badd-daf45f13bceb" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(7-6,1+3) \\  & ∼N(1,4).\end{aligned}

We want to find $P(Y\le 2.1).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 2.1) & =P(Z\le \frac{2.1-1}{2}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.55) \\  & =Φ(0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Φ(0.55)≈0.7088.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=2{X}_{1}-3{X}_{2} & ∼N(2{\mu }_{1}-3{\mu }_{2},4{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+9{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(4-3,28+36) \\  & ∼N(1,64).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =1$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{64}=8.$ 

We want to find $P(-4.6<Y<3.48).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.6<Y<3.48) & =P(\frac{-4.6-1}{8}<Z<\frac{3.48-1}{8}) \\  & =P(-0.70<Z<0.31) \\  & =P(Z<0.31)-P(Z<-0.70) \\  & =Φ(0.31)-Φ(-0.70)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.31) & ≈0.6217 \\ Φ(-0.70) & ≈0.2420.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.6<Y<3.48) & ≈Φ(0.31)-Φ(-0.70) \\  & ≈0.6217-0.2420 \\  & ≈0.3797.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186162290 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186158942 :answer-field/correct 17592186158943] ["question-f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/id #uuid "f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612"] ["question-f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/math-academy-id "q-109671"] ["question-f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/problem "If ${X}_{1}∼N(8,{40}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(30,{30}^{2})$ are independent and $Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2},$ calculate $P(-31\le Y\le 31).$ Round your final answer to two decimal places.

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(8-30,{40}^{2}+{30}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-22,2500).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-22$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{2500}=50.$ 

We want to find $P(-31\le Y\le 31).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-31\le Y\le 31) & =P(\frac{-31-(-22)}{50}\le Z\le \frac{31-(-22)}{50}) \\  & =P(-0.18\le Z\le 1.06) \\  & =P(Z<1.06)-P(Z<-0.18) \\  & =Φ(1.06)-Φ(-0.18)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.18) & ≈0.4286 \\ Φ(1.06) & ≈0.8554\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-31\le Y\le 31) & =Φ(1.06)-Φ(-0.18) \\  & ≈0.8554-0.4286 \\  & ≈0.43.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f962dd14-3b46-5fda-bac4-2a4b37326612" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6397adad-43cc-59f3-a17a-dddd5e5332c4" :answer-field/id #uuid are independent and $Y=5{X}_{1}+{X}_{2},$ calculate $P(Y<13.4).$ Round your final answer to two decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8643\,$ | $\,0.8665\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8849\,$ | $\,0.8869\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ |"] ["question-7e624f6f-227d-5bbb-b9ec-897830d915af" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),$ and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & =5{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}∼N(5{\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2},{5}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(5\cdot 1+4,25\cdot 0.4+6) \\  & ∼N(9,16).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =9$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{16}=4.$ 

We want to find $P(Y<13.4).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<13.4) & =P(Z<\frac{13.4-9}{4}) \\  & =P(Z<1.1) \\  & =Φ(1.1)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.1)≈0.8643.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y<13.4)≈0.86.
$$"] ["question-7e624f6f-227d-5bbb-b9ec-897830d915af" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c622c6db-0cfb-5314-962b-7b684cde7e09" :answer-field/id #uuid from a wooden blade covered with rubber on one side.  The weight of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $80\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $31\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weight of the rubber is normally distributed with a mean of $45\,\text{g}$ grams and a variance of $50\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ If one racket is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $128\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ |"] ["question-6718d3e2-fbcd-51c5-808c-744242ca4d81" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of the blade, and let $Y$ denote the weight of the rubber. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>128).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(80,31)$ and $Y∼N(45,50),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(80+45,31+50) \\  & ∼N(125,81).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =125$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{81}=9.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>128),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & =P(Z>\frac{128-125}{9}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.33) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.33) \\  & =Φ(0.33)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.33)≈0.6293.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & ≈1-Φ(0.33) \\  & ≈1-0.6293 \\  & ≈0.3707.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6718d3e2-fbcd-51c5-808c-744242ca4d81" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-23eb8fea-b998-548f-a61c-cbabe9a91a03" :answer-field/id #uuid The weight of a chicken is normally distributed with a mean of $1.5\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $0.1\,\text{kg}.$ The weight of a turkey is normally distributed with a mean of $8\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $0.4\,\text{kg}.$ If a chicken and a turkey are randomly selected, what is the probability that $5$ times the weight of the chicken is greater than the turkey's weight? You may assume that the weights are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ | $\,0.7852\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ | $\,0.8051\,$ | $\,0.8078\,$ | $\,0.8106\,$ | $\,0.8133\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ | $\,0.8315\,$ | $\,0.8340\,$ | $\,0.8365\,$ | $\,0.8389\,$ |"] ["question-e7f40d31-3891-595e-9dc0-80e5713161b9" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of a chicken, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a turkey. We want to find 

$$
P(5X>Y)=P(5X-Y>0).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(1.5,{0.1}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(8,{0.4}^{2}),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}5X-Y & ∼N(5\cdot 1.5-8,{5}^{2}\cdot {0.1}^{2}+{0.4}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(-0.5,0.41).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $5X-Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-0.5$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.41}.$

To find $P(5X-Y>0),$ we convert $5X-Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5X-Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0-(-0.5)}{\sqrt{0.41}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.78) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.78) \\  & =1-Φ(0.78)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.78)≈0.7823.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5X-Y>0) & ≈1-Φ(0.78) \\  & ≈1-0.7823 \\  & 0.2177.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e7f40d31-3891-595e-9dc0-80e5713161b9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-76f631c0-460f-51ec-9363-bfa37aabf5c3" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-bb6e266d-fd9f-5c8c-82b7-fde74e3fe145" :question/math-academy-id "q-175476"] ["question-bb6e266d-fd9f-5c8c-82b7-fde74e3fe145" :question/problem "A particular shop sells watermelons and melons. The weight of a watermelon is normally distributed with a mean of $10\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $4\,\text{kg}.$ The weight of a melon is normally distributed with a mean of $5\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{kg}.$ If one watermelon and one melon are randomly selected, what is the probability that the weight of the watermelon is more than $3$ times greater than the weight of the melon? You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ | $\,0.7123\,$ | $\,0.7157\,$ | $\,0.7190\,$ | $\,0.7224\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ | $\,0.7454\,$ | $\,0.7486\,$ | $\,0.7517\,$ | $\,0.7549\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ | $\,0.7852\,$ |"] ["question-bb6e266d-fd9f-5c8c-82b7-fde74e3fe145" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of a watermelon, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a melon. We want to find 

$$
P(X>3Y)=P(X-3Y>0).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(10,{4}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(5,{2}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X-3Y & ∼N(10-3\cdot 5,16+{3}^{2}\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(-5,52).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X-3Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =-5$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{52}.$

In order to find $P(X-3Y>0),$ we convert $X-3Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-3Y>0) & =P(Z>\frac{0+5}{\sqrt{52}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.69) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.69) \\  & =1-Φ(0.69)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.69)≈0.7549.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X-3Y>0) & ≈1-Φ(0.69) \\  & ≈1-0.7549 \\  & ≈0.2451.\end{aligned}
$$

times are normally distributed with a mean of $15$ minutes and a standard deviation of $3$ minutes. The conversation times are normally distributed with a mean of $10$ minutes and a standard deviation of $4$ minutes. The time to solve a problem is the sum of the waiting time and the conversation time. What is the probability that it took more than $30$ minutes to solve the problem of a randomly selected caller? You may assume that waiting and conversation times are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8413\,$ | $\,0.8438\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8643\,$ | $\,0.8665\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8849\,$ | $\,0.8869\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ |"] ["question-0c9343e5-40f1-5766-8346-83637c7ee445" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the waiting time, and let $Y$ denote the conversation time. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>30).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(15,{3}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(10,{4}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(15+10,{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(25,25).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =25$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{25}=5.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>30),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =P(Z>\frac{30-25}{5}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1) \\  & =1-Φ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1)≈0.8413.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =1-Φ(1) \\  & ≈1-0.8413 \\  & ≈0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0c9343e5-40f1-5766-8346-83637c7ee445" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b619dfd9-b2dd-59c0-870d-da366a920039" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-0c9343e5-40f1-5766-8346-83637c7ee445"] [17592186162297 :question/problem "A shop sells spray foam in small and large cans. The volume of liquid in a small can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.3\,\text{ltrs}$ and a standard deviation of $0.003\,\text{ltrs}.$ The volume of liquid in a large can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.6\,\text{ltrs}$ and a standard deviation of $0.008\,\text{ltrs}.$

The foam from a small can expands $40$ times its liquid volume after being sprayed in place, while the foam from a large can expands to $60$ times its liquid volume. 
If one small and one large can are randomly selected, what is the probability that the total foam volume from both cans after expanding is less than $49\,\text{ltrs}?$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9713\,$ | $\,0.9719\,$ | $\,0.9726\,$ | $\,0.9732\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |"] [17592186162297 :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the volume of liquid in a small can, and let $Y$ denote the volume of liquid in a big can. We want to find 

$$
P(40X+60Y<49).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(0.3,{0.003}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(0.6,{0.008}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}40X+60Y & ∼N(40\cdot 0.3+60\cdot 0.6,{40}^{2}\cdot {0.003}^{2}+{60}^{2}\cdot {0.008}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(48,0.2448).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $40X+60Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =48$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{0.2448}.$

In order to find $P(40X+60Y<49),$ we convert $40X+60Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(40X+60Y<49) & =P(Z<\frac{49-48}{\sqrt{0.2448}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<2.02) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.02) \\  & =Φ(2.02)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.02)≈0.9783.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(40X+60Y<49) & ≈Φ(2.02) \\  & ≈0.9783.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the probability that, after expanding, the total volume of foam is less than $49$ liters is $0.9783.$"] [17592186162297 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186158984 :answer-field/correct 17592186158986] [17592186163271 :tutorial/content "Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be *independent* random variables that are normally distributed with

$$
X_1\sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2).
$$

We can show that the random variable $Y = X_1\pm X_2$ is normally distributed, and

$$
Y =  X_1\pm X_2 \sim N(\mu_1\pm\mu_2, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2).
$$

We'll prove this in a separate lesson.

For example, if $X_1\sim N(2,3)$ and $X_2\sim  N(1,4)$ are independent, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{1}+{X}_{2} & ∼N(2+1,3+4)∼N(3,7),\end{aligned}
$$

 

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N(2-1,3+4)∼N(1,7).\end{aligned}
$$

 

When computing a sum or difference of normal random variables, there are a few things to watch out for:

- Firstly, when we compute the distribution of a *difference*, we subtract the means, but *add* the variances!

- Secondly, it is vital to check that $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent. Cases where $X_1$ and $X_2$ are *dependent* will be dealt with in future lessons."] [17592186163285 :tutorial/content "If $X_1\sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ and $X_2\sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$ are *independent* random variables and $a$ and $b$ are constants, we have

$$
aX_1+bX_2\sim N(a\mu_1+b\mu_2, a^2\sigma^2_1+b^2\sigma^2_2).
$$

For example, if $X_1\sim N(2,3)$ and $X_2\sim  N(1,4)$ are independent, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2} & ∼N(2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1,{2}^{2}\cdot 3+{3}^{2}\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(4+3,4\cdot 3+9\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(7,48),\end{aligned}
$$

 

and

$$
\begin{aligned}2{X}_{1}-3{X}_{2} & ∼N(2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot 1,{2}^{2}\cdot 3+{3}^{2}\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(4-3,4\cdot 3+9\cdot 4) \\  & ∼N(1,48).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186162166 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0] ["question-2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/id #uuid "2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a"] ["question-2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163499"] ["question-2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $6\,m,$ find the value of $k.$"] ["question-2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/worked-solution "![](images/9a/9ac139d8823f326f32869f308cb2d04cdc9e0d86dba7d4a11b66955afd665da3.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =k(\frac{(0)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(0)^{3}}{3})+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=6\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =k(\frac{(6)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(6)^{3}}{3})+6 \\ 0 & =k(324-360)+6 \\ 0 & =-36k+6 \\ 36k & =6 \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5a78871b-3da5-52c1-a57c-cb87914fafa1" :answer-field/id #uuid If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle."] ["question-3aa3a140-5e95-5af8-9fd5-684dff535064" :question/worked-solution "![](images/60/602ef5480fe59ccf921d17a19d10848a1a8a04a1fc3fb3181b8e9b17ebe81fad.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(7-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(7-x) & =0 \\ 7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(7-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(7-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(7(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{10})^{2} & =k(7(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+8 \\ 20 & =12k+8 \\ 12k & =12 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =14x-{x}^{2}+16 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(7)=\sqrt{-(7)^{2}+14(7)+16}=\sqrt{65}\,m/s
$$"] ["question-3aa3a140-5e95-5af8-9fd5-684dff535064" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-096d2af6-6379-5a37-9ed1-9857796a70e5" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(4-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=8\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle."] ["question-8f6a9cc3-415e-5254-bb6f-82cbdb814536" :question/worked-solution "![](images/73/73da2be2514373e6d0b1052f0eca21c339b4d826d38621faf72b3e251d7d8a95.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(4-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(4-2x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(4-2x) & =0 \\ 4-2x & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=2\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $3$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2k>0$ | $0$ | $-2k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=2\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(4-2x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(4-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(4(0)-(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(4x-{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=8\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =k(4(1)-{(1)}^{2})+8 \\ 32 & =3k+8 \\ 3k & =24 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8(4x-{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =32x-8{x}^{2}+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =-16{x}^{2}+64x+16 \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+4x+1}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(2)=4\sqrt{-(2)^{2}+4(2)+1}=4\sqrt{5}\,m/s
$$"] ["question-8f6a9cc3-415e-5254-bb6f-82cbdb814536" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-10849e2a-d2b8-5eda-a82b-458c2096cbcd" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-44a81c31-3d9d-5c47-8101-840c572bf6c4"] [17592186138439 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ff3d9c94-77b4-51bb-806f-e93681c391b2"] [17592186139596 :tutorial/content "The formula for the speed $S$ of a moving object is

$$
S=\dfrac{D}{T},
$$

where $D$ is the distance covered, and $T$ is the time taken.

For example, if a car travels a distance of $600\,\textrm{m}$ within a time of $30\,\textrm{s},$ at constant speed, then we can find the speed of the car using the formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{D}{T} \\  & =\frac{600}{30} \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

But what is the unit of speed? We can find it by substituting the units for distance and time into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{D}{T} \\  & =\frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}} \\  & =\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of the car is $20\,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.$ When the unit has a quotient like this, we say "meters *per* second.""] [17592186139597 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we can be given a formula with values whose units are not the standard ones we know.

For instance, suppose the formula for a person's popularity $P$ is given by

$$
P=\dfrac{2f}{s},
$$

where $f$ is the number of friends that person has, and $s$ is the number of siblings they have.

If we want to find the unit of popularity, then we need to substitute the units for the number of friends ($f$) and the number of siblings ($s$) into the formula.

- The units for the number of friends is '$\textrm{friends}$' since we say 'I have $5$ friends'.

- Similarly, the units for the number of siblings is '$\textrm{siblings}.$'

Substituting these units into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{2f}{s} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot \text{friends}}{\text{siblings}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{friends}}{\text{siblings}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the appropriate unit is $\dfrac{\textrm{friends}}{\textrm{siblings}}$, or "friends per sibling." Here we ignore the constant $2$ since it does not affect the units."] [17592186138590 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342" :question/id #uuid "58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342"] ["question-58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342" :question/math-academy-id "q-95331"] ["question-58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What is the mode of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}{e}^{-2x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342" :question/worked-solution "The mode of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ is the value of $x$ at the global maximum of $f(x).$

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $x\ge 0$ is $f(x)=4{x}^{2}{e}^{-2x}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =8x{e}^{-2x}-8{x}^{2}{e}^{-2x}=8{e}^{-2x}x(1-x),\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
8{e}^{-2x}x(1-x)\,⟹\,x=0,1.
$$

All of these critical points are within the interval $[0,\infty ),$ so we keep them.

- We've already considered the endpoint $x=0.$

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =4\cdot {0}^{2}{e}^{-0}=0 \\ f(1) & =4\cdot {1}^{2}{e}^{-2}=4{e}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f(1)=4{e}^{-2}.
$$

Therefore, the mode of $X$ is $1.$"] ["question-58a9cc29-6dde-501b-9df3-e43459e6c342" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d9ba206c-1c09-5d73-aac2-7ac035ea537b" ["question-3a2c219c-ccba-5ebb-bb19-2884f7df2aa0" :question/math-academy-id "q-95376"] ["question-3a2c219c-ccba-5ebb-bb19-2884f7df2aa0" :question/problem "Let $X$ be a random variable with the probability density function shown below. What are the modes of $X?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}{3\pi +2}, & 0\le x\le 3\pi  \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3a2c219c-ccba-5ebb-bb19-2884f7df2aa0" :question/worked-solution "The modes of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ are the values of $x$ at the global maxima of $f(x).$

To find the global maxima of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $0\le x\le 3\pi $ is $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1}{3\pi +2}.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3\pi +2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3\pi +2}=0\,⟹\,x=\frac{\pi }{2}+k\pi ,
$$

where $k$ is any integer.
Among these critical points, only three lie within the interval $[0,3\pi ].$ These are $x=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2},\frac{5\pi }{2},$ so we keep them all.

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=0,3\pi .$ So, these are critical points as well.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=0,\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2},\frac{5\pi }{2},3\pi :$

$$

$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest values are

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{5\pi }{2})=\frac{2}{3\pi +2}.

$f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{24}x,\, & 1\le x\le 7 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}$"] ["question-67c34d9e-6885-5f7c-abc2-3a7d77eaaea5" :question/worked-solution "The mode of a random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ is the value of $x$ at the global maximum of $f(x).$

To find the global maximum of $f(x),$ we find the critical points of $f(x)$ and then apply the candidates test.

First, we find the critical points.

- The piece of $f(x)$ defined on $1\le x\le 7$ is $f(x)=\frac{1}{24}x.$ Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are no solutions  of  ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- The derivative doesn't exist at the endpoints $x=1,7.$ So, these are critical points.

Now, we evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points $x=1,7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\frac{1}{24}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{24} \\ f(7) & =\frac{1}{24}\cdot 7=\frac{7}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compare all of the values above. The largest value is

$$
f(7)=\frac{7}{24}.
$$

Therefore, the mode of $X$ is $7.$"] ["question-67c34d9e-6885-5f7c-abc2-3a7d77eaaea5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e45ad8ad-0b7a-5fe0-93c7-2567d8e280e5" $$

are choosing an appropriate unit, we are not given any formula to use. 

This often occurs when we measure the **rate of change** of something. A rate of change measures how much something changes as we change something else.

In such cases, we can use a quotient to work out an appropriate unit. The numerator is what we measure the change of, and the denominator is what we change:

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}\textrm{what we measure the change of}}{\color{red}\textrm{what we change}}
$$

For instance, suppose that a newly opened store wants to measure the rate at which the number of customers increases each day.

We *measure the change* of the number of customers, as *we change* the number of days, so the most appropriate unit is

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}\textrm{customers}}{\color{red}\textrm{day}},
$$

or, customers per day."] [17592186138591 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186054365 :question/problem "Consider the following statement:

$$

$\,$ $B$ is {{field-2}},
$\,$ $A∧B$ is {{field-3}}."] ["question-e6fd19f6-d3a7-5978-9314-7283447a9c4c" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the following facts about the "and" $(∧)$ and "or" $(∨)$ logical connectives:

- The statement $A∧B$ is true if *both* $A$ and $B$ are true.

- The statement $A∨B$ is true if either $A$ is true, or $B$ is true, or *both* $A$ and $B$ are true.

In our case, $A$ is true, and $B$ is true. Therefore, the result is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{0.33\text{ is rational}}_{⏟}}_{A}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{3+1=2+2}_{⏟}}_{B} & \,\,≡\,\text{true}∧\text{true}≡\text{true}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e6fd19f6-d3a7-5978-9314-7283447a9c4c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-72f7a99b-3183-507b-ae1f-1ba5d0546e36" :answer-field/id #uuid $\,$ $(P∧Q)∧R$ is {{field-3}}."] [17592186055061 :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the following facts about the "and" $(∧)$ and "or" $(∨)$ logical connectives:

- The statement $A∧B$ is true if *both* $A$ and $B$ are true.

- The statement $A∨B$ is true if either $A$ is true, or $B$ is true, or *both* $A$ and $B$ are true.

In our case, $P$ is true, $Q$ is true, and $R$ is true. Therefore, $P∧Q$ is true, and the result is true:

$$"] [17592186055061 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186051859 :answer-field/correct 17592186051860] [17592186051862 :answer-field/correct 17592186051863] [17592186051865 :answer-field/correct 17592186051867] [17592186056005 :tutorial/content "A **compound statement** is a sentence that consists of two or more statements separated by logical connectors, such as the word "and" or the word "or."

For example, the following sentence is a compound statement:

$P: 2$ is an integer **and** $2$ is positive 

The first statement is "$2$ is an integer," and the second is "$2$ is positive." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "and."

The following sentence is also a compound statement:

$7$ is odd **or** $7$ is even 

In this case, the first statement is "$7$ is odd," and the second statement is "$7$ is even." These two statements are separated by the logical connector "or." 

We can express the logical connectives "and" and "or" using symbols:

- The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$\land$". Notice that it resembles "A" for "And."

- The word "or" is represented by the symbol "$\lor$".

Let's translate the following sentence into symbolic form:

$2$ is an integer **and** $2$ is positive 

To start, we introduce the letters $A$ and $B$ to denote each individual statement:

- $A:$ $2$ is an integer

- $B:$  $2$ is positive

Then, our sentence becomes

$$
\underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is an integer} }_A \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{2 \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is positive} }_B,
$$

that is, $A \land B.$

Finally, note the following terminology:

- The statement "$P$ and $Q$" is called the **conjunction** of the statements $P$ and $Q.$

- The statement "$P$ or $Q$" is called the **disjunction** of the statements $P$ and $Q.$"] [17592186056029 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the truth values of the logical connector "and". We have the following key idea:

*The statement $A \land B$ is true if $A$ is true **and** $B$ is true. Otherwise, it is false.* 

Let's determine the truth values of the following compound statement:

$2$ is positive **and** $2$ is even.

Writing this in symbols, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{2\text{ is positive}}_{⏟}}_{A}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{2\text{ is even}}_{⏟}}_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

or, simply

$$
A\land B.
$$

Since $A$ is true and $B$ is true, this compound statement is true:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧B≡\text{true}∧\text{true}≡\text{true}\end{aligned}
$$

In this context, the symbol "$\equiv$" means "is logically equivalent to." 

Let's now consider a similar compound statement but with the $2$ replaced with a $3$ in the second statement.

$$
\begin{aligned}{{2\text{ is positive}}_{⏟}}_{A}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{3\text{ is even}}_{⏟}}_{C}\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this symbolically as follows:

$$
A\land C
$$

Since $A$ is true and $C$ is false, this compound statement is false:

$$
\begin{aligned}A∧C≡\text{true}∧\text{false}≡\text{false}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186056072 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the truth values of the logical connector "or". We have the following key idea:

Let's consider some examples:

$$

Since $D$ and $C$ are both false, this compound statement is false:

$$
\begin{aligned}D∨C≡\text{false}∨\text{false}≡\text{false}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186054914 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186138282 :question/problem "Let $C,$ $D$ and $E$ be three collinear points such that $D$ is between $C$ and $E.$ If $CE = 8\,\text{cm}$ and $CD = 6\,\text{cm}$, find the length of $\overline{DE}$."] [17592186138282 :question/worked-solution "![](images/30/304a0de1777efb414a2504e22d53c1d15a5a0299196a7a9103a02491ff12e4c6.png)

The segment addition postulate states that

$$

Therefore, $DE = 2 \, \text{cm}$."] [17592186138283 :question/problem "Given the diagram shown below, what is the measure of $\overline{BC}?$

![](images/54/543c7c26c7d56d8ff10f4ece71b74bb5f04edf59fddb6f2c0df549848000abaf.png)"] [17592186138283 :question/worked-solution "The segment addition postulate can be applied to a set of more than three collinear points. In the given situation, it states that

![](images/3f/3fe1e3d1e6f89af1050d0437379a811eabb19212be36f0fecd91ddfaca2594ee.png)"] [17592186138284 :question/worked-solution "By the segment addition postulate, we have

$$

$$

To solve for $x,$ we can substitute the given information

$$

and then solve the resulting equation:

$$

$$"] [17592186138285 :question/problem "In the diagram below, the length of the line segment $\overline{AD}$ is $8d+12,$ $AB = 4d+4,$ and $C$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BD}.$ Express the length of $\overline{AC}$ in terms of $d.$

![](images/46/468fd25032d1a36e1658331053a33652cef7ff9ce3d9c95b729d6a7b7ebf1672.png)"] [17592186138285 :question/worked-solution "First, note that according to the segment addition postulate, we have

$$
AD = AB + BD,
$$

which, in turn, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}BD & =AD-AB \\  & =(8d+12)-(4d+4) \\  & =4d+8.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $C$ is the midpoint of $BD$, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =\frac{1}{2}BD \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4d+8) \\  & =2d+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =AB+BC \\  & =(4d+4)+(2d+4) \\  & =6d+8\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15" :question/id #uuid "da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15"] ["question-da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15" :question/math-academy-id "q-72037"] ["question-da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15" :question/problem "Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be three collinear points such that $PQ=7\text{ cm}$ and $QR=13\text{ cm}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P$ **cannot** lie between $Q$ and $R$

II. $Q$ **cannot** lie between $P$ and $R$

III. $R$ **cannot** lie between $P$ and $Q$"] ["question-da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15" :question/worked-solution "Let's check each statement.

If $P$ is between $Q$ and $R$, then, by the segments addition postulate, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =PQ+PR \\ 13 & =7+PR \\ 13-7 & =PR \\ PR & =6\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/d7/d7396a24e0e8884195184a4fca2b4e0fd9cfc2462249c7dc3a0c66901d062c5f.png)

Therefore, $P$ can lie between $Q$ and $R,$ so statement I is false.

If $Q$ is between $P$ and $R$, then again, by the segments addition postulate, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =PQ+QR \\  & =7+13 \\  & =20\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/2d/2dc899f0b5d08bf4a5b5e1833e62e4a3290c8da83dbd376ed51d185c1ed08e94.png)

Therefore, $Q$ can lie between $P$ and $R,$ so statement II is false.

If $R$ is between $P$ and $Q$, then, by the segments addition postulate, we would have:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =PR+QR \\ 7 & =PR+13 \\ PR & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

This can't happen since the length of a segment can't be negative. 

Therefore, $R$ cannot lie between $P$ and $Q,$ so statement III is true."] ["question-da73dbf4-60d5-5996-a49e-cd36cf80dd15" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be three collinear points such that $PQ=11\text{ cm}$ and $QR=16\text{ cm}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P$ **cannot** lie between $Q$ and $R$

II. $Q$ **cannot** lie between $P$ and $R$

III. $R$ **cannot** lie between $P$ and $Q$"] ["question-1734fbf3-8c46-59f6-b44b-50223df284ea" :question/worked-solution "Let's check each statement.

If $P$ is between $Q$ and $R$, then, by the segments addition postulate, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =PQ+PR \\ 16 & =11+PR \\ 16-11 & =PR \\ PR & =5\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/10/10a73ef77e6f4367b971465ab6be0a4decdb8a36a2931944fbe10be11c92475f.png)

Therefore, $P$ can lie between $Q$ and $R,$ so statement I is false.

If $Q$ is between $P$ and $R$, then again, by the segments addition postulate, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =PQ+QR \\  & =11+16 \\  & =27\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/7b/7b8d7c69c2a8d20e3c9a7e06a5cc5d3d456b117f4e7d7ce708cacf27fece0d68.png)

Therefore, $Q$ can lie between $P$ and $R,$ so statement II is false.

If $R$ is between $P$ and $Q$, then, by the segments addition postulate, we would have:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =PR+QR \\ 11 & =PR+16 \\ PR & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

This can't happen since the length of a segment can't be negative. 

Therefore, $R$ cannot lie between $P$ and $Q,$ so statement III is true."] ["question-1734fbf3-8c46-59f6-b44b-50223df284ea" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ![](images/95/956f9b2c979f06897b09119b089ced903e095d72136e64b9ea52e946fba41544.png)

As indicated in the diagram, the distances between the points are

$$
\begin{aligned}AB=4\,cm,\,BC=2\,cm,\,AC=6\,cm.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we be sure that the points are collinear? To answer this, we use the **segment addition postulate**.

The postulate states the following: 

*Three points are collinear if and only if the largest distance between two of them is equal to the sum of the other two distances.*

Here, the largest distance is $AC,$ so the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear *if and only if*

$$
AC=AB + BC.
$$

Substituting the given information $AC=6\,\mathrm{cm},$ $AB=4\,\mathrm{cm},$ and $BC=2\,\mathrm{cm}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =AB+BC \\ 6 & =4+2 \\ 6 & =6.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This is a true statement, so the three points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are indeed collinear.

**Note:** The postulate works in both directions:

- If the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear then $AC= AB + BC.$

- If $AC= AB + BC$ then the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear."] [17592186139636 :tutorial/content "Given two of the three distances between three collinear points, we can calculate the third distance using the segment addition postulate. 

To demonstrate, consider the collinear points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ below.

![](images/3b/3b1bc383e8d570f9dc33346e6f4ae04377e3c5c4c0d0e53abe07b0aacd9bb3e6.png)

We are given two of the distances:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB=3\,cm,\,AC=5\,cm\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the third distance, $BC,$ using the segment addition postulate.

First, we state the equation and substitute the known quantities $AB=3$ and $AC=5,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =AB+BC \\ 5 & =3+BC\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for $BC$ by subtracting $3$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =3+BC \\ BC & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance between the points $B$ and $C$ is $2\,\textrm{cm}.$"] [17592186138602 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0] ["question-a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e" :question/id #uuid "a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e"] ["question-a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-96118"] ["question-a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e" :question/problem "Given the singular value decomposition $A=UΣ{V}^{T},$ where $A$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, which of the following statements are true?

II. $U$ is an orthogonal matrix

III. $Σ$ is an orthogonal matrix"] ["question-a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $m\times n$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m\times m$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, $U$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the matrix $U$ in the singular value decomposition $UΣ{V}^{T}$ must be orthogonal.

- Statement III is false. The matrix $Σ$ must be diagonal but not necessarily orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""] ["question-a0773915-2806-5187-a512-1daa0afdcd4e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d36a171f-653b-5a9e-b0c3-ea8ba71c938e" $$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|?$"] ["question-6179c8a4-6c68-54e8-a44c-27a0976388cb" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$ So, the second column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=16.$ 

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 5 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 6 \\ 6 & 34\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-16I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-16I=[\begin{aligned}18 & 6 \\ 6 & 34\end{aligned}]-16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}]
$$

- Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we get 

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
|{v}_{12}|+|{v}_{22}|=|-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}|+|\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}|=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}.
$$"] ["question-6179c8a4-6c68-54e8-a44c-27a0976388cb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5d79fe0b-3705-52ed-9f17-ed653d7b53f0" :answer-field/id #uuid where ${v}_{i}$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

$$
