["question-9582267b-adc4-536b-9335-9619155f3b19" :question/math-academy-id "q-140646"] ["question-9582267b-adc4-536b-9335-9619155f3b19" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$"] ["question-9582267b-adc4-536b-9335-9619155f3b19" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=64,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-64I & =[\begin{aligned}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{aligned}]-64[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-27 & -18 \\ -18 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-64I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}37 & -18 \\ -18 & 52\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}12 & -18 \\ -18 & 27\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)x=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{16}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-9582267b-adc4-536b-9335-9619155f3b19" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-20030bd4-6e8a-5215-b9ee-0ffa2a972515" :answer-field/id #uuid "20030bd4-6e8a-5215-b9ee-0ffa2a972515"] ["answer-90a84480-b5fe-5e99-a5ca-05d902ef19d8" :answer/id #uuid "90a84480-b5fe-5e99-a5ca-05d902ef19d8"] ["answer-90a84480-b5fe-5e99-a5ca-05d902ef19d8" :answer/type :answer.type/text] ["answer-90a84480-b5fe-5e99-a5ca-05d902ef19d8" :answer/value "$U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$

It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y$:

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+6v-8 &= 0 \\ 2u+6v &= 8 \\ 2u &= 8 - 6v \\ u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \\ u &= 4 - 3v \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2+3v &= 0 \\ 3v &= -2 \\ v &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}

$$

$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \\ 2u-6-6 &= 0 \\ 2u-12 &= 0 \\ 2u &= 12 \\ u &= 6 \end{aligned}

\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)
$$"] [17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y &= 4 \\
x + (x - 2) &= 4 \\
2x - 2 &= 4 \\
2x &= 6 \\
x &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3$. But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x - 2 \\
y &= 3 - 2 \\
y &= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as

$$
\left(3, 1\right)
$$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A}
$$

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 4}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ cannot have a negative singular value.

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186416485 :question/id #uuid "e69dd032-aa5c-5891-a7fc-97b84703e88a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95261"} {:db/id 17592186416486 :question/id :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix ![](images/85/85f9ccea6cd39f07174651d07316218edf50041f9d373e22cdaedf0c779caaf3.svg)" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$  

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )^{2}-(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$

$$

$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda [(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4)] & =0 \\ -\lambda ({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}(\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{5} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{0}=0 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 3819} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186184968 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185322 :tutorial/content "Recall that the singular values of a real matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :tutorial/id #uuid "6230f35e-b526-5e84-be30-86c8cdcbd301" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(10-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +100-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =16,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

17592186134917 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135015 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we wish to evaluate the expression $\sqrt x + 3$ for the value $x=9.$ This type of expression is called a **radical expression** because it contains the radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom 0}.$ Remember that $\sqrt x$ means "the positive square root of the number $x.$" 

To evaluate this expression at the given value, we replace $x$ with $9$ in the given expression and simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x}+3 & = \\ \sqrt{9}+3 & = \\ \sqrt{{3}^{2}}+3 & = \\ 3+3 & = \\ 6\end{aligned}
$$

**Important:** You may have heard somewhere that $\sqrt{9} = \pm 3,$ because $(-3)^2=9$ and $(3)^2 = 9.$ However, when we write down $\sqrt{9},$ we *always* mean "the positive square root of $9$".

If we want the negative square root of $9$, we write $-\sqrt{9} = -3.$ Sometimes, we want both, in which case we would write $\pm\sqrt{9}=\pm 3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :question/problem "Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x=-3{x}^{3} \\ 5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $5x.$ We can factor out the $5x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{3}-40{x}^{2}+35x & =0 \\ 5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression ${x}^{2}-8x+7$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x({x}^{2}-8x+7) & =0 \\ 5x(x-1)(x-7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and $x=7.$"} {:db/id 17592186234025 :question/id #uuid "ed0dfccb-ca71-51c6-8509-751b260b91e1" :question/math-academy-id :topic/math-academy-id 480} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186074645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075006 :tutorial/content "A **polynomial equation** is an equation that can be written in the form

$$
P_n(x)=0,
$$

where $P_n(x)$  is a polynomial of degree $n.$
A **cubic equation** is a polynomial equation of degree $n=3.$

To solve a polynomial equation with no constant term, we factor the polynomial part using the greatest common factor.
Once we've done that, we can apply the zero product rule to the resulting factors.

For instance, consider the cubic equation $x^3-x=0.$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $x^2-1$ using the difference of squares formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ x(x+1)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, we conclude that the solutions are ${\color{red}x=0},$ ${\color{blue}x = -1},$ and ${\color{purple}x=1}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid given that
${\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362275 :question/id #uuid "920d3899-d202-5cde-aad8-d129368027e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-98189"} {:db/id 17592186388027 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Calculate 
${\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t$
given that
${\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨-4,\,-6,\,4⟩$
and
${\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨9,\,9,\,-6⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-(-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨9,\,9,\,-6⟩+⟨-4,\,-6,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,\,3,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459243 :question/id #uuid "626ec44a-73a5-5e9b-9066-3e6a39d1e10e" :question/math-academy-id "q-98214"} {:db/id 17592186459259 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find ${\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t$ 
given that 
${\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t=6\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ 
and 
$c=i-2\,j+2\,k.$" :question/worked-solution "The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-2\,j+2\,k)\times (6\,i-4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-6+8)i-(3-12)j+(-4+12)k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+8\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186440629 :question/id #uuid "42e2902f-b402-5b6e-826c-93f62fddd9ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-129293"} {:db/id 17592186440632 :question/id #uuid 17592186120790 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121079 :tutorial/content "Given a vector-valued function $\mathbf f(t)$ that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ the *rule for reversal of integration limits* states the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{b}^{a}f(t)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "43078f08-37bf-59a3-8462-3b3efc865eb1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5177 :tutorial/title "The Rule for Reversal of Integration Limits"} :step/id #uuid "660b20a9-f073-51b0-a1b7-e72f161ebfb3" :step/math-academy-id 32530 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120789}} {:db/id 17592186120791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121080 :tutorial/content "Given a vector-valued function $\mathbf f(t)$ that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b]$ and $p \in (a,b),$ the *adjacent intervals rule* states the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{p}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{p}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ef0617f3-7ee0-5300-8795-10adbdc19d3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5178 :tutorial/title "The Adjacent Intervals Rule"} :step/id #uuid "84aafb0e-a1fc-506a-aa26-8b23e04c1756" :step/math-academy-id 32531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120978}} {:db/id 17592186120792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121081 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ is a vector-valued function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b]$ and $\mathbf c$ is a constant vector. 
Then, the *products rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}[c\cdot f(t)]\text{d}t=c\cdot ({\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}[c\times f(t)]\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2531e67a-b5ed-5052-a97f-34abca386c58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5179 :tutorial/title "The Product Rules"} :step/id #uuid "60fca522-e8ee-530d-9936-cc7ec084b35f" :step/math-academy-id 32532 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120979}} {:db/id 17592186120976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186120995 :tutorial/content "Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3d07bd2-8d66-5645-a140-c638f5e9f002" $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ef0617f3-7ee0-5300-8795-10adbdc19d3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5178 :tutorial/title "The Adjacent Intervals Rule"} :step/id #uuid "84aafb0e-a1fc-506a-aa26-8b23e04c1756" :step/math-academy-id 32531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120978}} {:db/id 17592186120790 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121079 :tutorial/content "Given a vector-valued function $\mathbf f(t)$ that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ the *rule for reversal of integration limits* states the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{b}^{a}f(t)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{p}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{p}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

Then, the *products rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}[c\cdot f(t)]\text{d}t=c\cdot ({\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}[c\times f(t)]\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2531e67a-b5ed-5052-a97f-34abca386c58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5179 :tutorial/title "The Product Rules"} :step/id #uuid "60fca522-e8ee-530d-9936-cc7ec084b35f" :step/math-academy-id 32532 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120979}} {:db/id 17592186121081 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ is a vector-valued function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b]$ and $\mathbf c$ is a constant vector. 
Then, the *products rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}[c\cdot f(t)]\text{d}t=c\cdot ({\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}[c\times f(t)]\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2531e67a-b5ed-5052-a97f-34abca386c58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5179 :tutorial/title "The Product Rules"} {:db/id 17592186120979 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119982 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119552 :question/id #uuid "1d356bbb-b4ad-5730-9bd1-7f3cd151f96f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3021"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c8ee97e-f2b0-587e-9171-8008f1e0c4aa" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048954} {:db/id 17592186049132}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120179} {:db/id 17592186120181} {:db/id 17592186265708} {:db/id 17592186265709} {:db/id 17592186265710} {:db/id 17592186302129} {:db/id 17592186302176} {:db/id 17592186302198} {:db/id 17592186319235} {:db/id 17592186362280} {:db/id 17592186440629} {:db/id 17592186440632} {:db/id 17592186440634} {:db/id 17592186459225} {:db/id 17592186459307}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rules"} :step/id #uuid "7a2a2545-f4a7-5b95-93cf-cc4160242986" :step/math-academy-id 9894} {:db/id 17592186120995 :tutorial/content "Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3d07bd2-8d66-5645-a140-c638f5e9f002" :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5e79a91b-c479-53da-9f06-59c082fa4187" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution"}] :question/problem "Solve the following system of equations:
${x - y = 4; x + 2y = 16$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - y &= 4 \\
x &= 4 + y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} x+2y &=16 \\ (4+y) + 2y &=16 \\ 4+3y &=16 \\ 3y &=12 \\ y &=4 \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into

$$
x=4+y
$$

, then we can find the value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned} x &= 4 + y \\ &= 4 + (4) \\ &=8 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4)$."} {:db/id 17592186048678} {:db/id 17592186050622} {:db/id 17592186074030 :question/id #uuid "acc0a44e-6eb6-5a95-a139-3841ec88693b" :question/math-academy-id "q-171690"} {:db/id 17592186074172 :question/id #uuid "963fb1bc-3f29-5c06-94a9-37168b40e1c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-4133"} {:db/id 17592186074185 :question/id #uuid "5c71bd6b-b9a3-5587-89f4-a14a2c760bc2" :question/math-academy-id "q-5179"} {:db/id 17592186233560 :question/id #uuid "ba03c851-f080-5b98-bcba-fc2174ffc663" :question/math-academy-id "q-167194"} {:db/id 17592186233567 :question/id #uuid "d104504e-e7b5-56df-8154-499bbc1d3f80" :question/math-academy-id "q-167210"} {:db/id 17592186233574 :question/id #uuid "6afc1799-60d6-5f69-94a5-994731079a93" :question/math-academy-id "q-167226"} {:db/id 17592186073753 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073446 :question/id #uuid "707504e8-a367-5dc2-a663-371a9dcf7224" :question/math-academy-id "e-13010"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4352698-7af7-5d74-9c3a-0f951c3e6078" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186073997 :question/id #uuid "833a2ed3-b37f-5ade-bd6a-5fdaf64b6506" :question/math-academy-id "q-12444"} {:db/id 17592186073998 :question/id #uuid "90bf8b55-699c-5e18-b484-90473cb6a72f" :question/math-academy-id "q-12457"} {:db/id 17592186074047 :question/id #uuid "a7c18dc6-0363-5db7-9c51-22de1db359fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-18483"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution"} {:db/id 17592186073446 :question/id #uuid "707504e8-a367-5dc2-a663-371a9dcf7224" :question/math-academy-id "e-13010" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186073753 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4352698-7af7-5d74-9c3a-0f951c3e6078" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution"}] :question/problem "Solve the following system of equations:

${2u + 9v - 6 = 0; 2u + 6v - 8 = 0$" :question/worked-solution "Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
{2u + 9v - 6 = 0(1); 2u + 6v - 8 = 0(2)
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+6v-8 &= 0 \\ 2u+6v &= 8 \\ 2u &= 8 - 6v \\ u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \\ u &= 4 - 3v \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2+3v &= 0 \\ 3v &= -2 \\ v &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute

$$
v=-\dfrac{2}{3}
$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\ 2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \\ 2u-6-6 &= 0 \\ 2u-12 &= 0 \\ 2u &= 12 \\ u &= 6 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and

$$
v=-\dfrac{2}{3}
$$

, which can be written as

$$
\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186073997 :question/id #uuid "833a2ed3-b37f-5ade-bd6a-5fdaf64b6506" :question/math-academy-id "q-12444"} {:db/id 17592186073998 :question/id #uuid "90bf8b55-699c-5e18-b484-90473cb6a72f" :question/math-academy-id "q-12457"} {:db/id 17592186074047 :question/id #uuid "a7c18dc6-0363-5db7-9c51-22de1db359fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-18483"} {:db/id 17592186048216} {:db/id 17592186048646} {:db/id 17592186048873} {:db/id 17592186048975} {:db/id 17592186048991} {:db/id 17592186049144} {:db/id 17592186049198} {:db/id 17592186049869} {:db/id 17592186050326} {:db/id 17592186050365} {:db/id 17592186050564} {:db/id 17592186050661} {:db/id 17592186050754} {:db/id 17592186050788} {:db/id 17592186050926} {:db/id 17592186050964} {:db/id 17592186050974} {:db/id 17592186050984} {:db/id 17592186051014} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186074657} :activity/id #uuid "7809af08-83ac-5450-986d-2614a3fd22d3" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048826 :topic/id #uuid "c375d3cc-e398-5a47-a69f-ddc853431752" :topic/math-academy-id 487} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186074657 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
{x + y = 4; x - 2 = y
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y &= 4 \\
x + (x - 2) &= 4 \\
2x - 2 &= 4 \\
2x &= 6 \\
x &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3$. But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x - 2 \\
y &= 3 - 2 \\
y &= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as

$$
\left(3, 1\right)
$$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1e8cb2d-3d4e-5cb9-8947-2bd9deb11b89" {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073923} {:db/id 17592186074657 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
{x + y = 4; x - 2 = y
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y &= 4 \\
x + (x - 2) &= 4 \\
2x - 2 &= 4 \\
2x &= 6 \\
x &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3$. But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x - 2 \\
y &= 3 - 2 \\
y &= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as

$$
\left(3, 1\right)
$$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable." :tutorial/id #uuid "e1e8cb2d-3d4e-5cb9-8947-2bd9deb11b89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8131 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "413b9b90-7693-5568-a868-970271a5a258" :step/math-academy-id 197419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074658}} {:db/id 17592186075033 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

"Consider the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[-1,1]\to R$ and its subset $B={f\in C[-1,1]\,|\,f(1)=f(-1)}.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $B$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $B$ is a subspace of $C[-1,1]$
- **IV.** $B$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-1,1]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in B,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(1) & =f(1)+g(1) \\  & =f(-1)+g(-1) \\  & =(f+g)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\in B$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}(kf)(1) & =kf(1) \\  & =kf(-1) \\  & =(kf)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $B$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

- **I.** $E$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $E$ is a subspace of $C[-2,2]$
- **IV.** $E$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-2,2]$

*Hint: $f$ is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x\in [-2,2].$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in E,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(-x) & =f(-x)+g(-x) \\  & =f(x)+g(x) \\  & =(f+g)(x)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $E$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\in E$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}(kf)(-x) & =kf(-x) \\  & =kf(x) \\  & =(kf)(x)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $E$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186378355 :question/id #uuid "ff663474-9982-50d0-b983-22c1b4e4d38b" :question/math-academy-id "q-107144"} {:db/id 17592186378362 Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $K$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $K$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $K$ is a subspace of $C[0,1]$
- **IV.** $K$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,1]$

*Hint: $f$ is a constant function if $f(x)=\text{constant}$ for all $x\in [0,1].$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, the functions $f(x)=x+2$ and $f(x)=-x-1$ are in $K$, however

$$
(f+g)(x)=1
$$

for all $x\in [0,1]$ and hence $f+g$ is a constant function. 
So, $K$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, the product of the scalar zero by any function is the constant function zero. So, $K$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $K$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186446399 :question/id #uuid "33331944-2261-5079-a111-5d0397fe6a4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-107146"} {:db/id 17592186446401 :question/id #uuid "7e86fe7b-82ad-5786-81ac-5ea87b6be543" :question/math-academy-id "q-107145"} {:db/id 17592186493915 :question/id #uuid "3ec301c4-26d6-5f2a-9132-b21928f5ee67" :question/math-academy-id "q-94638" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25ce7efb-3ad5-579b-809f-0dd2e31fe7e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "IV only" :db/id 17592186493451} {:answer/id #uuid "87f00bc1-a093-5b90-a9c9-83e2777d88d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III only" :db/id 17592186493604} {:answer/id #uuid "aca0bca7-0e7a-58b7-a3c4-843dab2110e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and IV only" :db/id 17592186493662} {:answer/id #uuid "be1fae9a-76f7-5ae7-af20-eb786be794c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493703} {:answer/id #uuid "f14395c6-36b4-5cb6-8085-7a9935a781a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and IV only" :db/id 17592186493780}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493451} :answer-field/id #uuid "28ce3e2a-2275-50a0-b25b-b9f3436f743c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493812}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the vector space $C[0,3]$ of all continuous functions $f:[0,3]\to R$ and its subset $N$ containing all functions that return a nonzero value at exactly one point in $[0,3].$

II. $N$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $N$ is a subspace of $C[0,3]$

IV. $N$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,3]$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f({a}_{1})\ne 0$ and $g({a}_{2})\ne 0,$ where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are distinct points in $[0,3],$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f({a}_{1})+g({a}_{1}) & \ne 0 \\ f({a}_{2})+g({a}_{2}) & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)+g(x)\ne 0$ at two distinct points. So, $N$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(a)\ne 0$ for some $a\in [0,3],$ and $k=0,$ then

$$
kf(x)=0
$$

 
for any $x\in [0,3].$ So, $N$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $N$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186124590 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124401 :question/id #uuid "7fed39de-7304-52a0-a94d-e55703175d7d" II. $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $C$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}ka & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $C.$ So, $C$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $C$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186125155 :question/id #uuid "bff3a0b0-c74a-55ac-a94b-e3a390164777" :question/math-academy-id "q-43772"} {:db/id 17592186244021 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $A={[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a,b\in R}.$  

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $A$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}]$ are two matrices from $A,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & {a}_{1}+{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

 
which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}]$ is an element of $A$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ b & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & ka \\ kb & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $A$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186244023 :question/id #uuid "72b2f218-4463-5051-8c3b-5d02162b5905" :question/math-academy-id "q-107115"} {:db/id 17592186244025 "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $E$ containing all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $\alpha A$ where $A$ is some fixed $2\times 2$ matrix and $\alpha \in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $E$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $E$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $E$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}={\alpha }_{1}A$ and ${A}_{2}={\alpha }_{2}A$ are two matrices from $E,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & ={\alpha }_{1}A+{\alpha }_{2}A=({\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{2})A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $B=\alpha A$ is an element of $E$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kB & =k\alpha A=(k\alpha )A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $E$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186329725 :question/id #uuid "76fb5f0d-770c-53e0-bb5c-9231d8688147" :question/math-academy-id "q-43776"} {:db/id 17592186360461 "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $B={[\begin{aligned}0 & a \\ 1-a & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a\in R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $B$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $B$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}={A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a matrix from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $k=2,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =2[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a matrix from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186360463 :question/id #uuid "4c523e99-06d7-537c-99b6-2e21ff3e81b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-94629"} {:db/id 17592186360464 :question/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R,$ and its subset $S$ containing $2\times 2$ matrices that are not invertible. 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $S$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $S$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $S$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. For example, if ${A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],$ then
${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ each contain a row consisting only of zeros, so they are not invertible. However,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

is invertible. So, $S$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, if $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix that is not invertible then $det(A)=0$ and therefore for all $\alpha \in R$ 

$$
det(\alpha A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot det(A)={\alpha }^{2}\cdot 0=0.
$$

Therefore,  $S$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $S$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186380284 :question/id #uuid "3e8696fa-a30e-5b2e-a6f9-20152471933a" :question/math-academy-id "q-94621"} {:db/id 17592186380291 in the variable $t$ of degree at most $3,$ and its subset $B=\{a{t}^{3}+bt+1\,|\,a,b\in R\}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $B$ is closed under polynomial addition

II. $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication

III. $B$ is a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$

IV. $B$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}_{3}[t]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, if $f(t)=g(t)=t+1,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =(t+1)+(t+1) \\  & =2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, if $f(t)=t+1$ and $k=2,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =2(t+1)=2t+2,\end{aligned}
$$

which is not a polynomial from $B.$ So, $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $B$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "af81d6e6-3cad-5c8a-99a9-13bc107158af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :topic/math-academy-id 1907} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125348 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125762 :tutorial/content "Given a vector space $V$, any subset $H$ of $V,$ which is itself a vector space, is called a **subspace** of $V$. 

Fortunately, we do not need to check all vector space axioms to determine whether a subset of some vector space is a subspace. Instead, we only need to check the **subspace criterion**, which states the following:

*A subset $H$ of a vector space $V$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if $H$ is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. That is to say, both of the following conditions hold:*

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lie in $H$, then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ also lies in $H$. Formally,*

$$
\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in H.
$$

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ lies in $H$, then $k \cdot \mathbf{u}$ also lies in $H$ for any scalar  $k$. Formally,* 

$$
k \in \mathbb{R}, \,\mathbf{u} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  k\cdot\mathbf{u} \in H.
$$

For example, consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$ containing all polynomials of degree at most $3,$ along with the subset 

$$
A = \{ at^2 \:|\: a \in \mathbb{R} \}.
$$

Is $A$ a subspace? Let's check the two subspace criterion conditions: 

- Suppose $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2$ and $p_2(t)=a_2 t^2$ are two polynomials from $A$. Summing the two polynomials, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}_{1}(t)+{p}_{2}(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{2})+({a}_{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $p_1(t)+p_2(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

- If $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2 \in A$ and $k \in \mathbb{R},$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}k{p}_{1}(t) & =k({a}_{1}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{(k{a}_{1})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $kp_1(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

Since both conditions hold, we conclude that $A$ is a subspace $\mathbb{R}_3[t].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4274a05d-d402-5dfc-a339-e5a6b5a8e5b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3205 :tutorial/title {:db/id 17592186125595 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125858 :tutorial/content "Let's now look at an example of a subset of a vector space that is not a subspace.

Consider the vector space $\mathbb R_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2,$ and its subset 

$$
B = \big\{ at+b \: | \: a,b  \in\mathbb{Z} \big\}.
$$

Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

- $B$ is closed under polynomial addition. Indeed, suppose that $f(t)=a_1t+b_1$ and $g(t)=a_2t+b_2$ are two polynomials from $B.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)+g(t) & =({a}_{1}t+{b}_{1})+({a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}) \\  & =({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+{b}_{2}),\end{aligned}
$$

which is a polynomial from $B$ since $a_1+a_2$ and $b_1+b_2$ are in $\Bbb Z.$

- $B$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication. As a counterexample, consider $f(t)=t$ and $k=0.5,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kf(t) & =0.5t,\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial from $B,$ because $0.5 \notin \Bbb Z.$

Fortunately, we do not need to check all vector space axioms to determine whether a subset of some vector space is a subspace. Instead, we only need to check the **subspace criterion**, which states the following:

*A subset $H$ of a vector space $V$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if $H$ is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. That is to say, both of the following conditions hold:*

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ lie in $H$, then their sum $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$ also lies in $H$. Formally,*

$$
\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} \in H.
$$

- *If $\mathbf{u}$ lies in $H$, then $k \cdot \mathbf{u}$ also lies in $H$ for any scalar  $k$. Formally,* 

$$
k \in \mathbb{R}, \,\mathbf{u} \in H \quad\Rightarrow\quad  k\cdot\mathbf{u} \in H.
$$

For example, consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_3[t]$ containing all polynomials of degree at most $3,$ along with the subset 

$$
A = \{ at^2 \:|\: a \in \mathbb{R} \}.
$$

Is $A$ a subspace? Let's check the two subspace criterion conditions: 

- Suppose $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2$ and $p_2(t)=a_2 t^2$ are two polynomials from $A$. Summing the two polynomials, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}_{1}(t)+{p}_{2}(t) & =({a}_{1}{t}^{2})+({a}_{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{({a}_{1}+{a}_{2})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $p_1(t)+p_2(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

- If $p_1(t)=a_1 t^2 \in A$ and $k \in \mathbb{R},$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}k{p}_{1}(t) & =k({a}_{1}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={{(k{a}_{1})}_{⏟}}_{a\in R}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Thus, $kp_1(t)$ is a polynomial of the form $at^2,$ which belongs to $A$.

Since both conditions hold, we conclude that $A$ is a subspace $\mathbb{R}_3[t].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4274a05d-d402-5dfc-a339-e5a6b5a8e5b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3205 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c9024def-0495-5d67-911a-9b23824e8187" :step/math-academy-id 653353 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125595}} {:db/id 17592186125762 :tutorial/content "Given a vector space $V$, any subset $H$ of $V,$ which is itself a vector space, is called a **subspace** of $V$.

:question/math-academy-id "q-43775" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $E$ containing all $2\times 2$ matrices of the form $\alpha A$ where $A$ is some fixed $2\times 2$ matrix and $\alpha \in R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $E$ is closed under matrix addition
- **II.** $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $E$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- **IV.** $E$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If ${A}_{1}={\alpha }_{1}A$ and ${A}_{2}={\alpha }_{2}A$ are two matrices from $E,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & ={\alpha }_{1}A+{\alpha }_{2}A=({\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{2})A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $B=\alpha A$ is an element of $E$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}kB & =k\alpha A=(k\alpha )A,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a matrix from $E.$ So, $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $E$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "50493f64-ffe9-5fa7-9d7b-f97ed6fe8636" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481717}} {:db/id 17592186481708 :step/content {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-107147" :question/problem "Consider the vector space $C[0,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to R$ and its subset $K$ containing all nonconstant functions.

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $K$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $K$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $K$ is a subspace of $C[0,1]$
- **IV.** $K$ is **not** a subspace of $C[0,1]$

*Hint: $f$ is a constant function if $f(x)=\text{constant}$ for all $x\in [0,1].$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, the functions $f(x)=x+2$ and $f(x)=-x-1$ are in $K$, however

$$
(f+g)(x)=1
$$

for all $x\in [0,1]$ and hence $f+g$ is a constant function. 
So, $K$ is *not* closed under addition.

- Statement II is false. For example, the product of the scalar zero by any function is the constant function zero. So, $K$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $K$ is *not* a subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""} :step/id #uuid "67adba61-524d-57c0-85ec-fefe501262e8"} {:db/id 17592186481710 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360467 :question/answer-fields $$
\begin{aligned}kB & =k\alpha A=(k\alpha )A,\end{aligned}

$$

$$
kf(x)=0
$$

 
for any $x\in [0,3].$ So, $N$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication.

:question/math-academy-id "q-43779" :question/problem "Consider the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of all continuous functions $f:[-1,1]\to R$ and its subset $B={f\in C[-1,1]\,|\,f(1)=f(-1)}.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $B$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $B$ is a subspace of $C[-1,1]$
- **IV.** $B$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-1,1]$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in B,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(1) & =f(1)+g(1) \\  & =f(-1)+g(-1) \\  & =(f+g)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\in B$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}(kf)(1) & =kf(1) \\  & =kf(-1) \\  & =(kf)(-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $B$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "876842ab-2531-5a55-8715-683cc46f3d77" :step/next {:db/id 17592186494008}} {:db/id 17592186494030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125154 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8536f8a6-1bfc-5275-95ca-8a1fda0afe28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186123525} {:answer/id #uuid "b659c777-4549-54ab-9f1f-bae85db6256b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and IV only" :db/id 17592186123526} {:answer/id #uuid "5da722ba-7c66-52bf-862c-fc5ad59257b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "IV only" :db/id 17592186123527} {:answer/id #uuid "64f059cc-f403-5120-b592-b5803d968b43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III only" :db/id 17592186123528} {:answer/id #uuid "79c277c4-a05b-5a16-ab06-0142128ff522" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and IV only" :db/id 17592186123529}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186123528} :answer-field/id #uuid "856e0bc2-ed8c-5746-a814-6831d1a835e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123524}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "027d54ca-a5e1-5f8e-b0e8-aea8a3580062" :question/math-academy-id "q-43770" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $C=\{[\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\,|\,a\in R\}.$

continuous functions $f:[-2,2]\to R$ and its subset $E$ containing all even functions.

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $E$ is closed under function addition
- **II.** $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication
- **III.** $E$ is a subspace of $C[-2,2]$
- **IV.** $E$ is **not** a subspace of $C[-2,2]$

*Hint: $f$ is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x\in [-2,2].$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. If $f(x),g(x)\in E,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(-x) & =f(-x)+g(-x) \\  & =f(x)+g(x) \\  & =(f+g)(x)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $E$ is closed under addition.

- Statement II is true. If $f(x)\in E$ and $k\in R,$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}(kf)(-x) & =kf(-x) \\  & =kf(x) \\  & =(kf)(x)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $E$ is closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement III is true, while statement IV is false. $E$ is a subspace because it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "ef5989bf-617a-54c7-bbc7-9e531c1f1c5b"} {:db/id 17592186494029 :step/content {:db/id 17592186329727 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [2,3].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348423 :question/id #uuid "a3840370-2613-5223-99ab-f0ad1e415b85" :question/math-academy-id "q-80626"} {:db/id 17592186348424 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186445488 :question/id #uuid "c4bacfe6-30e7-5d9e-a1c2-df77375c3f7b" :question/math-academy-id "q-129955"} {:db/id 17592186129172 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$

a Rectangular Domain"} :step/id #uuid "f422ea91-80bb-5373-9f64-444e0646074d" :step/math-academy-id 22627} {:db/id 17592186130068 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130397 :tutorial/content "Remember that the definite integral of a single-variable function can be split up over adjacent subintervals. That is to say,

$$
\int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_b^c f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

Suppose that a domain $D$ is the union of two adjacent sub-domains $D_1$ and $D_2$ (meaning that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are non-overlapping regions that could share a common border). Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$

This property can be generalized if $D$ is split into a finite number $n$ of sub-domains (where $n>2$):

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \cdots + \iint\limits_{D_n}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bc4e2a2c-afd3-57e1-ac95-737c568153b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4258 :tutorial/title "Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "5249980b-32b5-5965-880e-a7948ef2b5f3" :step/math-academy-id 25886 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130069}} {:db/id 17592186130069 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129188 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129007 :question/id #uuid "1c227b12-d40b-53a8-b568-b7bd380acbee" :question/math-academy-id "e-7023"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8505beff-75b8-57bf-9312-e0fcf32f44fd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129873} {:db/id 17592186129874} {:db/id 17592186265799} {:db/id 17592186348431} {:db/id 17592186348432} {:db/id 17592186380887} {:db/id 17592186380894} {:db/id 17592186380901} {:db/id 17592186382455} {:db/id 17592186394030} {:db/id 17592186419654} {:db/id 17592186445485} {:db/id 17592186445487}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "bca38320-513b-5017-88bb-f5d1a8c6013e" :step/math-academy-id 25887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130070}} {:db/id 17592186130070 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130398 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region $R.$ The definite integral of $f(x)$ over $R$ is not affected by whether the region $R$ is open or closed.

For example, consider the function $f(x) = 1,$ and define the regions $R = [0,1]$ and $R' = (0,1).$ Integrating $f(x)$ over $R$ and $R'$ gives the same result:

$$
\int_R f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{R'} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{0}^1 \,\textrm d x = 1
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the rectangles formed by $f(x),$ namely $[0, 1]\times [0,1]$ and $(0, 1)\times (0,1),$ have the same area. 

We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result. 

For example, the double integral of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ over both $R=[0,1] \times [0,1]$ and over $R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)$ will give the same result:

$$
\iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the *volumes* of the shapes formed by $f(x,y)$ over the regions $R$ and $R'$ are the same.

Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate $f(x,y)$ over any of the following regions:

$$
(0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots
$$

The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f51d452-a229-5d76-885e-0fe84f787707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4311 :tutorial/title "Open and Closed Regions of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "45710b0f-af68-5a20-b9ce-c5ecc560f4e5" :step/math-academy-id 26202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130034}}] :activity/title "Properties of Double Integrals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129345} {:db/id 17592186130030 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130375 :tutorial/content "Double integrals have properties that are similar to the properties of definite integrals of single-variable functions:

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bc4e2a2c-afd3-57e1-ac95-737c568153b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4258 :tutorial/title "Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "5249980b-32b5-5965-880e-a7948ef2b5f3" :step/math-academy-id 25886 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130069}} {:db/id 17592186130034 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129172 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128991 :question/id #uuid "0cb8fa8a-5be1-5f53-bfde-5acf325f6332" :question/math-academy-id "e-6108"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8059a197-e9fb-5306-8eed-62c0cea88f33" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534} {:db/id 17592186050432}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129849} {:db/id 17592186129872} {:db/id 17592186265804} {:db/id 17592186265805} {:db/id 17592186265807} {:db/id 17592186265808} {:db/id 17592186351279} {:db/id 17592186380908} {:db/id 17592186382193} {:db/id 17592186382462} {:db/id 17592186445483} {:db/id 17592186445486}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Additivity Over a Rectangular Domain"} :step/id #uuid "f422ea91-80bb-5373-9f64-444e0646074d" :step/math-academy-id 22627} {:db/id 17592186130397 :tutorial/content "Remember that the definite integral of a single-variable function can be split up over adjacent subintervals. That is to say,

$$
\int_a^c f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_b^c f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

In the same way, the definite integral of a two-variable function can be split up over adjacent sub-domains.

Suppose that a domain $D$ is the union of two adjacent sub-domains $D_1$ and $D_2$ (meaning that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are non-overlapping regions that could share a common border). Then, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$

This property can be generalized if $D$ is split into a finite number $n$ of sub-domains (where $n>2$):

$$
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_{D_1}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \iint\limits_{D_2}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A + \cdots + \iint\limits_{D_n}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bc4e2a2c-afd3-57e1-ac95-737c568153b8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4258 :tutorial/title "Additivity of Double Integrals"} {:db/id 17592186130069 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129188 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129007 :question/id #uuid "1c227b12-d40b-53a8-b568-b7bd380acbee" :question/math-academy-id "e-7023"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8505beff-75b8-57bf-9312-e0fcf32f44fd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129873} {:db/id 17592186129874} {:db/id 17592186265799} {:db/id 17592186348431} {:db/id 17592186348432} {:db/id 17592186380887} {:db/id 17592186380894} {:db/id 17592186380901} {:db/id 17592186382455} {:db/id 17592186394030} {:db/id 17592186419654} {:db/id 17592186445485} {:db/id 17592186445487}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Additivity of Double Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "bca38320-513b-5017-88bb-f5d1a8c6013e" :step/math-academy-id 25887 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130070}} {:db/id 17592186130070 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130398 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region $R.$ The definite integral of $f(x)$ over $R$ is not affected by whether the region $R$ is open or closed.

For example, consider the function $f(x) = 1,$ and define the regions $R = [0,1]$ and $R' = (0,1).$ Integrating $f(x)$ over $R$ and $R'$ gives the same result:

$$
\int_R f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{R'} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \int_{0}^1 \,\textrm d x = 1
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the rectangles formed by $f(x),$ namely $[0, 1]\times [0,1]$ and $(0, 1)\times (0,1),$ have the same area. 

We have a similar property for double integrals too. We can either include or exclude the boundaries of the integration regions without affecting the result. 

For example, the double integral of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ over both $R=[0,1] \times [0,1]$ and over $R'=(0,1) \times (0,1)$ will give the same result:

$$
\iint\limits_{\large R} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R'} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \ \text{d}A
$$

Intuitively, this is true because the *volumes* of the shapes formed by $f(x,y)$ over the regions $R$ and $R'$ are the same.

Moreover, we'd get the same result if we were to integrate $f(x,y)$ over any of the following regions:

$$
(0,1] \times [0,1], \quad [0,1) \times [0,1], \quad (0,1) \times [0,1], \quad \ldots
$$

The same idea applies to double-integrals over non-rectangular boundaries, too." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f51d452-a229-5d76-885e-0fe84f787707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4311 :tutorial/title "Open and Closed Regions of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "45710b0f-af68-5a20-b9ce-c5ecc560f4e5" :step/math-academy-id 26202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130034}} {:db/id 17592186130398 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're integrating a single-variable function over a region $R.$ The definite integral of $f(x)$ over $R$ is not affected by whether the region $R$ is open or closed.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-2){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{2}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[{y}^{3}]_{2}^{3} \\  & =(e-1)({3}^{3}-{2}^{3}) \\  & =19(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1-3x{y}^{2}}{x}\,\text{d}A=1-19(e-1)=20-19e.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8b0d3e0f-96a8-599d-92f9-04874e8f5b73" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419656}} {:db/id 17592186419656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129873 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60fb41e7-e3b3-596b-9de2-56afe6dd5f07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346193} {:answer/id #uuid "6c9ef82d-4456-5d25-ad26-90ed8d7f4c1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346295} {:answer/id #uuid "705f8690-2e07-5932-b07c-8089792360e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{T}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346333} {:answer/id #uuid "9666eb71-130a-59fc-8098-2ba78743d703" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186346666} {:answer/id #uuid "c006f721-3d51-5d16-a6a8-1b8222268571" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{T}(x+{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{U}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A" :db/id 17592186347011}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186346193} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ef450e5-1471-5ba8-8652-38a2e4337160" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186347853}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3e01cd29-3b44-5c08-bc75-551f046b44dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-80452" :question/problem "![](images/ed/ed0be2aca8d43d733e91f3a8feaaca0649957dcbd516a8218b1e7dea136170d8.png)

$$"} :step/id #uuid "f337f9e2-418d-5c24-9790-11f1621a546e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "168581f2-f17c-5d44-a38c-f447560aea9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4"
